Corticosteroids do not change outcome in bronchiolitis and are not recommended in the RCH guideline. Dexamethasone has a role in croup, not bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Intubation is reserved for true respiratory failure (severe acidosis, recurrent apnoeas, exhaustion despite HFNC). A pH of 7.30 with mild hypercapnia and a tiring but alert infant is an indication to escalate to HFNC before considering invasive ventilation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Hypertonic saline has inconsistent evidence and is not first-line escalation in RCH guidance. Routine chest physiotherapy is contraindicated in bronchiolitis as it does not improve outcomes and can worsen distress. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Severe croup is defined by stridor at rest with marked retractions, decreased air entry or agitation. Treatment is oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (0.15 mg/kg is mild-moderate) PLUS nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose). Minimum observation 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose because of rebound stridor.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-moderate, 0.6 mg/kg for severe
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 is a FLAT dose, not weight-based
Observe minimum 3 hours after last nebulised adrenaline
explanation.pearls: If a child needs more than 2-3 doses of nebulised adrenaline within an hour, escalate to ICU for closer monitoring or consideration of airway support; rebound is a normal phenomenon, not a treatment failure marker.

options.rationale: 0.15 mg/kg is the RCH dose for mild to moderate croup. This child has biphasic stridor at rest with tracheal tug and agitation - severe croup. He needs the higher dose AND nebulised adrenaline, with longer observation. Discharge after 1 hour is unsafe. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral or IV dexamethasone is not tolerated, but it is not the first-line monotherapy in severe croup. Dexamethasone (oral or IV) with concurrent nebulised adrenaline is the standard combination. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Severe croup (stridor at rest with marked respiratory distress or agitation) is treated with dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally (or IV/IM if oral not tolerated) AND nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 (a flat dose, not per kg). Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline nebuliser because of rebound. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

There is no drooling, no tripod position, no muffled voice and no marked toxicity to suggest epiglottitis. Manipulation including IV cannulation in a child with possible epiglottitis is contraindicated. Empirical antibiotics are not part of croup management. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Intubation is reserved for impending or actual airway obstruction unresponsive to medical therapy. Initial management with steroid plus nebulised adrenaline resolves the majority of severe croup. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months is treated with azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days and requires admission for monitoring of apnoea, cyanotic spells and secondary complications. Household contacts (especially under-6-month-olds and pregnant women) need prophylaxis. Erythromycin is avoided under 1 month because of pyloric stenosis association. Treatment reduces infectivity even if started in the paroxysmal phase.
key_points: Azithromycin preferred over erythromycin in under-1-month-olds (pyloric stenosis)
Admit all under-6-month-olds with pertussis for monitoring
Household contact prophylaxis essential
explanation.pearls: Marked lymphocytosis (>20 x10^9/L) with normal CRP in an infant with paroxysmal cough is highly suggestive of pertussis; raise the index of suspicion even before PCR returns.

options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with paroxysmal cough and observed apnoea or cyanosis must be admitted regardless of how well they appear between spells, because apnoea, secondary pneumonia and pulmonary hypertension can develop rapidly. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Empirical treatment should not wait for PCR confirmation when clinical suspicion is high (paroxysmal cough, cyanotic spells, marked lymphocytosis, contact, unimmunised). Delaying treatment delays infectivity reduction and prolongs household risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Ceftriaxone covers neither Bordetella pertussis nor the clinical picture, which is consistent with pertussis rather than bacterial pneumonia (clear chest, no infiltrate, classic paroxysms with lymphocytosis). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

RCH and the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommend macrolide treatment for pertussis in infants under 6 months. Azithromycin (10 mg/kg daily for 5 days) is preferred in this age group because erythromycin in under-1-month-olds is associated with pyloric stenosis - azithromycin is the safer macrolide. Treatment reduces infectivity and household contacts (especially the older brother and pregnant women) need prophylaxis. Admission is mandatory for monitoring of apnoea and oxygen need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Erythromycin in infants under 1 month is associated with pyloric stenosis and is no longer preferred. Azithromycin is the recommended macrolide for young infants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal children, those under 2 years, or with recurrent episodes warrants immediate antibiotic therapy because of the high risk of chronic suppurative otitis media. First-line is high-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days; recurrence within 30 days or failure escalates to amoxicillin-clavulanate. Watchful waiting is reserved for non-severe AOM in over-2-year-olds without these risk factors.
key_points: Aboriginal children with AOM are not candidates for watchful waiting
Recurrence within 30 days of amoxicillin escalates to amoxicillin-clavulanate
5-day course for under 2 years, longer courses NOT routinely needed
explanation.pearls: Chronic suppurative otitis media prevalence in remote Aboriginal communities can exceed 10-20%; aggressive treatment of acute episodes plus regular ENT follow-up is the cornerstone of preventing conductive hearing loss and educational impact.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for non-severe acute otitis media in healthy children over 2 years; Aboriginal children, those under 2 years, those with severe symptoms or recurrent episodes warrant immediate antibiotics because of high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cefuroxime is not the preferred first or second-line agent for acute otitis media in Australian guidelines. Amoxicillin at high dose or amoxicillin-clavulanate are preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Azithromycin has poor activity against drug-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common organism in acute otitis media after recent amoxicillin exposure, and is not recommended as a first or second-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intramuscular benzathine penicillin is used for syphilis, group A strep eradication and rheumatic fever prophylaxis. It is not a treatment for acute otitis media; it does not provide useful middle-ear concentrations of beta-lactamase-resistant cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

When acute otitis media recurs within 30 days of amoxicillin OR fails high-dose amoxicillin, Australian guidelines escalate to amoxicillin-clavulanate to cover beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Aboriginal children with recurrent AOM are prioritised for immediate treatment because of high rates of chronic suppurative otitis media. The 5-day course is appropriate for this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal impaction is treated with macrogol 3350 (PEG with electrolytes) at disimpaction dose for 3 to 7 days, followed by maintenance dose for at least 6 months. Lactulose alone is often insufficient. Behavioural toileting program and education about withholding are essential adjuncts. Red flags (failure to thrive, delayed meconium, neurological signs) require structural workup.
key_points: Disimpaction with macrogol before maintenance therapy
Maintenance for at least 6 months to prevent relapse
Lactulose is inferior to macrogol for disimpaction
explanation.pearls: Soiling between hard stools is overflow soiling, not encopresis as a primary behavioural issue; treating the constipation resolves the soiling without the need for behavioural therapy in most cases.

options.rationale: Functional constipation with a palpable faecal mass on examination indicates impaction, which must be treated with a disimpaction regimen before maintenance therapy can work. Macrogol 3350 (PEG with electrolytes) at escalating disimpaction dose for 3 to 7 days is first-line in Australian and international guidance, followed by maintenance dose for at least 6 months to prevent relapse. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Lactulose has already failed for 8 weeks. Stimulant laxatives like senna may be added later in maintenance, but disimpaction with macrogol is the priority when there is a palpable faecal mass. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Hirschsprung disease typically presents in the first weeks of life with delayed passage of meconium or in the first year with failure to thrive. A normally growing 5-year-old with classic withholding behaviour does not require structural imaging. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Phosphate enemas are reserved for failure of oral disimpaction and have significant electrolyte risks (hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia) in young children. Anaesthetic disimpaction is a last resort. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Anorectal manometry is used when an organic cause is suspected (Hirschsprung disease, anorectal dysmotility). In the absence of red flags, functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis and treated empirically with macrogol first. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Congenital hyperinsulinism is diagnosed by hypoglycaemia with detectable insulin, suppressed ketones (BOHB below 1.5 mmol/L) and low free fatty acids, plus a glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min. First-line therapy is diazoxide with chlorothiazide. Non-responders undergo 18F-DOPA PET to identify focal versus diffuse disease - focal lesions are cured by partial pancreatectomy while diffuse disease requires near-total pancreatectomy with subsequent diabetes risk.
key_points: Glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min is the threshold for diagnosing hyperinsulinism
Diazoxide opens KATP channels; chlorothiazide is added for synergy and to counter fluid retention
18F-DOPA PET differentiates focal from diffuse disease in diazoxide non-responders
explanation.pearls: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is on the differential for hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia in a macrosomic baby - look for macroglossia, ear pits/creases, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, and order methylation studies of 11p15.5 if features are present.

options.rationale: Persistent glucose infusion rates above 10 mg/kg/min in a macrosomic infant with detectable insulin during hypoglycaemia, low ketones and low free fatty acids confirms congenital hyperinsulinism. Simply pushing more dextrose treats the symptom not the cause and risks fluid overload and hyperosmolality - pharmacotherapy is now indicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Congenital hyperinsulinism is the diagnosis: persistent hypoglycaemia with glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min, detectable insulin during a low BSL, suppressed ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate below 1.5 mmol/L) and suppressed free fatty acids. Diazoxide opens KATP channels on beta cells to suppress insulin secretion; chlorothiazide is added to counter sodium and fluid retention and may potentiate the effect. Diazoxide responsiveness suggests a focal or diffuse KATP channel disorder amenable to medical therapy; non-response triggers 18F-DOPA PET to localise focal lesions for partial pancreatectomy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Cortisol of 380 nmol/L during stress is appropriate; hydrocortisone is not indicated and does not address hyperinsulinism. Stress-dose steroid would only apply if adrenal insufficiency were proven. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)
Surgery is reserved for diazoxide-unresponsive focal disease confirmed by 18F-DOPA PET. A medical trial is essential before surgical referral. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Infant-of-diabetic-mother hyperinsulinism usually resolves by 48 to 72 hours and does not require a glucose infusion rate above 10 mg/kg/min. Persistent requirement at this level points to congenital hyperinsulinism rather than transient. The biochemistry (low ketones, low FFA, detectable insulin) confirms this. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Cyanosis with failed hyperoxia test (PaO2 fails to rise above 100 mmHg or SpO2 below 90% in FiO2 1.0) indicates duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms/kg/min and arrange urgent echocardiography. TGA classically shows an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and equal pre and post-ductal saturations because mixing depends on PFO/ASD plus PDA. Lower-dose PGE1 (10 ng/kg/min) reduces apnoea while maintaining ductal patency.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia test = cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise
TGA: equal pre and post-ductal saturations, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette
Prostaglandin E1 10 ng/kg/min - lower doses reduce apnoea risk
explanation.pearls: Equal pre and post-ductal saturations rule out simple right-to-left ductal shunting (which gives a saturation gradient); they suggest fixed intracardiac mixing as in TGA. A balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) is often the first definitive intervention before arterial switch.

options.rationale: The hyperoxia test has already failed (SpO2 rose only marginally with FiO2 1.0). Continuing to push oxygen has minimal benefit in fixed right-to-left shunting and may even close the ductus in some duct-dependent lesions, worsening cyanosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

There is no tachypnoea or respiratory distress and the chest X-ray shows a cardiac silhouette, not the ground-glass appearance of RDS. Cyanosis without distress and a failed hyperoxia test points to cyanotic congenital heart disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Cyanosis with a failed hyperoxia test, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette and equal pre and post-ductal saturations is highly suggestive of transposition of the great arteries (TGA) with restricted intracardiac mixing. The duct must be kept open with prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) starting at 10 nanograms/kg/min until urgent echo confirms the diagnosis and a balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) or arterial switch can be planned. Lower starting doses (5 to 10 ng/kg/min) reduce apnoea risk compared with the older 50 ng/kg/min dose. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Vitamin K should already have been given routinely; diuretics treat pulmonary congestion but the issue here is fixed right-to-left shunt requiring ductal patency, not pulmonary overcirculation alone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Four-limb BPs have already been recorded as equal; coarctation typically presents with weak femoral pulses and right-arm-to-leg gradient, not equal pressures with cyanosis. Echocardiography is the first-line modality, not CT. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in 3 to 36-month-olds. Classic triad is intermittent severe colicky pain, palpable mass and redcurrant jelly stool, though most patients have only one or two features. Ultrasound (target sign) is diagnostic. First-line treatment is air enema reduction under fluoroscopy with surgical standby. Surgery is reserved for failure, perforation or shock.
key_points: Air enema reduction first-line, 80-95% success
Surgical standby mandatory because of 0.5-1% perforation risk
Surgery reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, or shock
explanation.pearls: Children under 3 months or over 5 years with intussusception have a higher rate of pathological lead point; in these atypical age groups, plan for CT or laparoscopic assessment after reduction even if reduction succeeds.

options.rationale: Conservative observation risks bowel ischaemia and perforation. Once intussusception is confirmed on ultrasound and there is no contraindication, reduction should proceed promptly. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Surgical reduction is reserved for failed pneumatic/hydrostatic reduction, peritonitis, free intraperitoneal air or shock. None of these are present, so a non-operative approach should be attempted first. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma) is more common in children over 2 years or recurrent cases; in a 9-month-old with classic presentation and ultrasound diagnosis, non-operative reduction is first-line and laparoscopy is reserved for failures or atypical cases. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Air enema (or hydrostatic) reduction with fluoroscopic guidance is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception, with success rates of 80 to 95%. Surgical standby is mandatory because of the 0.5 to 1% perforation risk during reduction. IV access, fluid resuscitation and theatre availability should be arranged before the procedure. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)
Antibiotic administration is appropriate adjunct but does not address the obstruction. The definitive next step is reduction (air enema), not observation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children carries a much higher risk of suppurative complications and chronic perforation than in non-Indigenous children. eTG departs from the watchful-waiting default and recommends prompt high-dose oral amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is for treatment failure or recurrent disease. Grommets and IM benzathine are not first-line acute treatments.
key_points: eTG: Aboriginal child with AOM gets antibiotics without delay
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg BD for 5 days first-line
Step up to amoxicillin-clavulanate if no response at 48-72 hours
Grommets for recurrent disease or persistent effusion with hearing loss
explanation.pearls: Higher 30 mg/kg twice-daily amoxicillin dose covers intermediately penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and is the AU standard for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is the default for non-severe acute otitis media in low-risk children, but Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have substantially higher rates of suppurative complications and chronic perforation, so eTG recommends prompt antibiotics rather than delayed prescribing in this group. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

First-line oral amoxicillin at the higher 30 mg/kg twice-daily dose for five days is the eTG-recommended regimen for acute otitis media in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children because of higher rates of chronic suppurative otitis media and pneumococcal disease. The dose covers intermediately penicillin-resistant pneumococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin, recurrent acute otitis media within 30 days, or concurrent purulent conjunctivitis. It is not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Grommets are considered after recurrent acute otitis media (three episodes in six months or four in a year) or chronic otitis media with effusion causing hearing loss greater than three months, not at the acute presentation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is used in remote settings for streptococcal pharyngitis prevention of rheumatic fever, not as first-line acute otitis media therapy where oral amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler with high cow's milk intake and fussy eating is overwhelmingly nutritional iron deficiency. Oral elemental iron at 3-6 mg/kg/day plus reduction of cow's milk to under 500 mL/day is first-line, with FBC review at 4 weeks. Endoscopy and electrophoresis are reserved for non-responders or atypical pictures. IV iron is reserved for malabsorption or intolerance.
key_points: Iron 3-6 mg/kg/day oral elemental iron is RCH-recommended dose
Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day to reduce displacement and occult loss
Reassess at 4 weeks; expect Hb rise ≥10 g/L
IV iron only for malabsorption or oral failure
explanation.pearls: Excess cow's milk above 500 mL/day in toddlers causes both iron displacement and microscopic enteric blood loss; capping intake is therapeutic, not just preventive.

options.rationale: RCH recommends oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day for established iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with classic dietary drivers, with concurrent reduction of cow's milk to under 500 mL daily because excess cow's milk both displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult enteric blood loss. Reassess at 4 weeks for haemoglobin rise of at least 10 g/L. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Endoscopy is not indicated when the dietary history and clinical picture explain the iron deficiency. Investigation for occult blood loss is reserved for failure to respond to iron replacement after 4-6 weeks of adherence, or atypical features such as failure to thrive or overt bleeding. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Thalassaemia trait is in the microcytic differential but is usually distinguished from iron deficiency by the Mentzer index (MCV/RBC), family history, ethnicity and ferritin. A clear nutritional history with low ferritin warrants empirical iron trial first; electrophoresis is reserved for cases with normal ferritin and persistent microcytosis. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

IV iron in children is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance of oral iron, or inflammatory bowel disease with ongoing losses. Oral iron is first-line in nutritional iron deficiency, with response expected by 4 weeks. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Dietary modification alone is insufficient once iron deficiency anaemia is established because the deficit requires replacement that cannot be met by diet within a reasonable timeframe. Oral iron supplementation plus dietary change is the standard approach. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis discharge requires SpO2 at or above 92% on room air for at least 4 hours including a sleep period, mild or absent work of breathing, feeding at or above 50% of normal, and reliable carers with safety-net access. Respiratory rate is not a discharge criterion. Steroids, repeat imaging, and home pulse oximetry are not used. Routine GP review at 1-2 days completes the plan.
key_points: SpO2 ≥92% RA for 4 hours including sleep is the RCH oxygenation criterion
Feeding ≥50% of normal is the hydration criterion
Tachypnoea persists for days and is not a discharge criterion
No role for steroids, repeat CXR, or home oximetry
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis discharge criteria are clinical: SpO2 92% on RA across a sleep period plus feeding at half of normal plus mild work of breathing plus reliable carers.

options.rationale: Home pulse oximetry is not routinely used after bronchiolitis discharge in Australia, and the criteria for discharge in this child are already met without it. The RCH pathway uses clinical and feeding criteria, not home monitoring. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Respiratory rate is not a discharge criterion in the RCH bronchiolitis pathway; persistent tachypnoea is expected for several days post-infection and does not preclude discharge if work of breathing is mild and feeding is adequate. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Corticosteroids do not alter the course of bronchiolitis in children under 12 months and are not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway. They have no role in discharge planning. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

RCH discharge criteria for bronchiolitis are met: SpO2 sustained at or above 92% on room air for at least 4 hours including a sleep period, taking at least 50% of feeds, mild or absent work of breathing, and reliable parents able to return. Routine GP follow-up at 1-2 days completes the safety net. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Routine repeat imaging or blood gas is not recommended in clinically improving bronchiolitis. Imaging at any stage is reserved for unexpected deterioration or diagnostic uncertainty. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: The RCH UTI imaging cascade recommends renal tract ultrasound after a first febrile UTI in infants under 6 months. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and not part of the RCH cascade for typical first UTI. Further imaging is added only for atypical features (poor response, non-E coli, abnormal ultrasound) or recurrent UTI. This case meets the under-6-month criterion regardless of antenatal scan history.
key_points: Under 6 months + first febrile UTI = ultrasound
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade after typical UTI
Atypical features (non-E coli, poor response, mass, raised creatinine) escalate imaging
Recurrent UTI with abnormal US triggers MCUG
explanation.pearls: RCH imaging cascade differs from NICE: AU practice uses ultrasound as the index investigation and reserves DMSA/MCUG for atypical or recurrent disease, not first typical UTI.

options.rationale: Although a typical first UTI in a child older than 6 months does not require routine ultrasound, this child is under 6 months which independently triggers ultrasound under the RCH guideline. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)
DMSA is part of the NICE pathway, not the RCH cascade. The RCH guideline does not routinely use DMSA after first typical UTI. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

MCUG is not part of the RCH cascade after a single typical UTI. It is reserved for recurrent UTI with abnormal ultrasound, or atypical features such as poor response to antibiotics or a non-E coli organism. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

RCH recommends renal tract ultrasound during the index admission for infants under 6 months with their first febrile UTI, OR when antenatal monitoring is not confirmed reliable. This child's antenatal scans are reported as normal but the under-6-month age alone meets the imaging criterion. Ultrasound assesses anatomy and excludes hydronephrosis or obstruction. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Cystoscopy is reserved for suspected posterior urethral valves in a male infant with antenatal hydronephrosis, poor stream, or palpable bladder. With normal antenatal scans and a typical UTI presentation this is not indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: HSP renal involvement appears within 6 months of presentation in up to 40% of children and is the main determinant of long-term outcome. RCH triggers paediatric nephrology referral for persistent proteinuria, hypertension, raised creatinine, or nephrotic syndrome. Steroids do not prevent HSP nephritis. Antihypertensives and ACE inhibitors are initiated by specialists after biopsy assessment.
key_points: HSP renal monitoring with serial urinalysis and BP for at least 6 months
Trigger for nephrology: persistent proteinuria, hypertension, raised creatinine
uPCR over 25 mg/mmol is significant; over 250 mg/mmol is nephrotic range
Steroids do not prevent or reliably treat HSP nephritis
explanation.pearls: HSP nephritis severity is dictated by biopsy histology, not clinical features alone; AU practice escalates early to paediatric nephrology when proteinuria with hypertension co-exist.

options.rationale: A urine protein:creatinine ratio of 88 mg/mmol is well above the nephrotic-range threshold of 250 and significantly above the upper limit of normal of 25; this level of proteinuria with co-incident hypertension at the 95th centile triggers paediatric nephrology referral, not reassurance. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Steroids in HSP are used for severe abdominal pain or arthritis and do not prevent or reliably treat HSP nephritis; treatment decisions for HSP nephritis follow renal biopsy histology and are guided by paediatric nephrology. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

RCH HSP follow-up triggers nephrology referral for any of: persistent proteinuria (uPCR over 25 mg/mmol beyond 4 weeks), hypertension, raised creatinine, or nephrotic syndrome. This child has proteinuria approaching nephrotic range with hypertension at the 95th centile and needs early renal biopsy planning. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

ACE inhibitors are commonly used in HSP nephritis with persistent proteinuria but the choice and dosing should be guided by a paediatric nephrologist after histology, not initiated in GP follow-up without specialist input. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

A spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is the recommended quantification in paediatric practice and 24-hour collection is impractical in young children. Specialist referral should not wait on additional confirmatory testing. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Threadworm (Enterobius vermicularis) is a common cause of perianal itch and secondary vulvovaginitis in girls. AU practice treats with oral mebendazole 100 mg single dose repeated at 2 weeks for the index case and all household members aged 6 months and over, plus hygiene measures. Topical antifungals do not treat threadworm. Vulvovaginitis from threadworm does not warrant protection referral without explicit suspicious features.
key_points: Tape test eggs are pathognomonic for Enterobius vermicularis
Mebendazole 100 mg single dose + repeat at 2 weeks; treat household
Hygiene: nail trimming, morning shower, hot wash linen
Vulvovaginitis is a common secondary feature in girls
explanation.pearls: The repeat dose at 2 weeks targets larvae that mature after the first dose (mebendazole has no larvicidal effect on eggs in utero); skipping it is the commonest treatment failure.

options.rationale: Treating only the index child misses the household reservoir; reinfection and ongoing symptoms are highly likely without simultaneous family treatment. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Threadworm is a common cause of childhood vulvovaginitis with characteristic itch and discharge. There is no clinical feature here triggering child protection referral; explicit features (recurrent unexplained STI, disclosure, anogenital injury) would prompt that pathway. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)
The vulval swab excludes candidiasis and the perianal tape confirms enterobiasis. Antifungal therapy does not treat threadworm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

AMH recommends treating the index case and all household members aged 6 months and older with mebendazole 100 mg single dose repeated at 2 weeks to interrupt the egg-laying cycle. Hygiene measures (nail trimming, daily morning shower, hot wash of bed linen and underwear) are essential adjuncts. The repeat dose targets larvae that mature after the first dose. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Albendazole is an alternative agent but a single dose without repeat allows larvae to mature and re-establish infection; the repeat at 2 weeks is essential. Treating the household is also required. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: DKA can cause abdominal pain that mimics surgical pathology and resolves with rehydration, but persistent focal signs with confirmatory imaging require surgical source control. The default 'rehydrate and re-examine' branch is the wrong branch when imaging is positive and signs persist. Insulin is continued through surgery and a glucose-containing fluid is added once blood sugars fall. CT is not first-line for paediatric appendicitis when ultrasound is diagnostic.
key_points: DKA can mimic acute abdomen; persistent focal signs plus positive imaging override
Restore circulation and start K+ replacement before theatre
Continue insulin infusion intra-operatively; add glucose if BSL <14 mmol/L
Ultrasound is first-line paediatric appendicitis imaging
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA with focal RIF signs, an ultrasound positive for appendicitis flips the textbook default - resuscitate, do not normalise pH, then proceed to theatre with insulin infusion running.

options.rationale: The ultrasound is diagnostic for appendicitis and the abdominal signs are not explained by DKA alone (no lipase rise, focal RIF rebound persisting after fluid resuscitation, leucocytosis above DKA baseline). RCH and ANZCA paediatric peri-operative DKA guidance support proceeding to theatre once circulation is restored and potassium is replacing, with continuous insulin infusion plus glucose-containing fluid to prevent hypoglycaemia. Source control is the priority; pH need not normalise pre-operatively. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

The ultrasound finding of a non-compressible 9 mm appendix with surrounding fluid is diagnostic of acute appendicitis; persisting tenderness with rebound and guarding despite 2 hours of resuscitation, plus a white cell count of 22 and normal lipase, points to true surgical pathology rather than ketoacidosis-related abdominal pain. Delay until DKA resolution risks perforation. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)
Stopping insulin worsens ketoacidosis and is contraindicated; insulin infusion is continued through and after surgery in known DKA. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Non-operative management of paediatric appendicitis is investigational and not recommended in a child with established DKA, drowsiness, and ultrasound evidence of complicated appendicitis; surgery is the primary management. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

Ultrasound has already confirmed appendicitis in this child; CT adds ionising radiation and contrast load in established DKA without changing the management decision. Paediatric appendicitis imaging is ultrasound-first in AU practice. (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months has high apnoea, pneumonia, and death rates. A characteristic triad of paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, and post-tussive emesis or apnoea, with marked lymphocytosis, is enough to start macrolides empirically while PCR returns. Azithromycin is preferred under 1 month given infant pyloric stenosis risk reported with erythromycin. Notification to public health and post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts (including non-immunised household members) is required. Antenatal maternal vaccination at 20-32 weeks reduces severe infant disease.
key_points: Admit any infant under 6 months with proven or suspected pertussis for apnoea monitoring
Azithromycin preferred under 1 month (pyloric stenosis risk with erythromycin)
Notifiable disease - contact tracing and prophylaxis for vulnerable contacts
Antenatal maternal booster at 20-32 weeks is the primary prevention strategy
explanation.pearls: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the AU first-line for treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis in infants under 1 month.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with paroxysmal cough, whoop, and desaturations require admission for monitored apnoea risk; discharge underestimates progression and contact-tracing duty. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

Infant pertussis with desaturation, lymphocytosis, and household exposure mandates admission for apnoea observation; azithromycin shortens infectivity and is preferred under 1 month over erythromycin (pyloric stenosis risk reduced). Droplet precautions plus public health notification are required. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis; RCH CPG: Pertussis)
Amoxicillin has no activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are required. There is also no wheeze documented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Beta-agonists do not modify pertussis paroxysms; bronchodilators are reserved for documented reactive airways. Short-stay observation is also inappropriate for an infant under 6 months with apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

Sepsis screen is reasonable in unwell infants under 28 days, but afebrile lymphocytosis with whoop after exposure favours pertussis; ceftriaxone is also contraindicated under 1 month if jaundiced or receiving calcium and is not the targeted treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: Inhaled foreign body in toddlers presents as a witnessed choking episode followed by an asymptomatic period before localised signs reappear. Peanuts and dry pulses are the most frequent culprits. Expiratory or decubitus films demonstrate air trapping from a ball-valve effect; a normal inspiratory film does not exclude the diagnosis. Definitive management is rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic, and the index of suspicion - not imaging - drives the referral.
key_points: Witnessed choke plus focal monophonic wheeze is bronchoscopy until proven otherwise
Normal inspiratory CXR does not exclude foreign body
Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic - flexible is diagnostic only
Peanuts under 3 years - dietary education at every well-child check
explanation.pearls: On expiratory or lateral decubitus chest X-ray, the obstructed side stays hyperinflated and the mediastinum shifts away - the opposite of the side you might expect.

options.rationale: Beta-agonists and steroids are appropriate for asthma but do not address a retained foreign body, and delay risks distal infection and granulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

Back blows are reserved for the conscious choking child with complete airway obstruction; this child is settled, talking, and oxygenating. The retained foreign body still needs definitive removal. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

Witnessed choking with localised wheeze, focal reduced air entry, and expiratory hyperinflation with mediastinal shift on the right is a classic ball-valve foreign body. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic by an experienced ENT or paediatric airway team is the diagnostic and therapeutic intervention; flexible bronchoscopy is diagnostic only. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)
Most aspirated organic foreign bodies are radiolucent and CT can be falsely reassuring; the diagnosis is clinical and the next step is bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

Antibiotics and physiotherapy are not the answer to a retained foreign body and do not relieve obstruction; missed foreign bodies lead to post-obstructive pneumonia and bronchiectasis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time-critical diagnosis. Sudden severe scrotal pain, vomiting, an absent cremasteric reflex, and a high-riding, horizontal testis is sufficient clinical evidence to proceed to theatre without ultrasound. Salvage rates fall sharply after 6 hours of ischaemia; bilateral orchidopexy is performed at exploration because the contralateral side shares the bell-clapper anatomy. Differentials (epididymo-orchitis, torsion of testicular appendage, idiopathic scrotal oedema) typically have a more gradual onset and preserved cremasteric reflex.
key_points: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis - never delay surgery for imaging
Salvage falls after about 6 hours of ischaemia
Bilateral orchidopexy performed at exploration (bell-clapper is bilateral)
Absent cremasteric reflex is the most specific bedside sign
explanation.pearls: Sudden-onset scrotal pain in a teenage boy with an absent cremasteric reflex goes straight to theatre - ultrasound is for equivocal cases, not classic ones.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Classic torsion features (sudden pain, absent cremasteric reflex, high-riding horizontal lie, vomiting) within the salvage window of about 6 hours mandate immediate exploration; imaging that delays surgery reduces salvage rates. Contralateral fixation is performed at the same operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Doppler can miss intermittent or partial torsion and any imaging delay reduces salvage; clinical features here are diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)

Epididymo-orchitis usually has a more gradual onset, dysuria, preserved cremasteric reflex, and Prehn sign relief on elevation; antibiotic empirical cover here delays surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Manual detorsion can temporise pain in delayed presentations while theatre is readied but is never definitive; orchidopexy is still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)
Watchful waiting risks irreversible ischaemia; the window to salvage is approximately 6 hours from onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotal pain)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management is plotted on age- and risk-adjusted nomograms. A value above the phototherapy line at day 5 in a well infant warrants admission for intensive phototherapy and continued breastfeeding with adequate feeding support. Conjugated bilirubin over 15% of total (or over 20 micromol/L) raises concern for biliary atresia and prompts urgent paediatric assessment. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy features (hypertonia, opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, lethargy refractory to feeding) demand immediate exchange.
key_points: Plot bilirubin on age-and-risk nomogram - thresholds are time-dependent
Continue breastfeeding with support during phototherapy where possible
Conjugated > 15% of total or > 20 micromol/L: think biliary atresia, urgent referral
Send DAT, group, FBC, reticulocyte count when above phototherapy line
explanation.pearls: Severe weight loss (>10% of birth weight by day 5) plus jaundice usually reflects insufficient breast milk intake; lactation support is essential alongside phototherapy.

sources.label: Australian College of Midwives Position Statement

options.rationale: The total serum bilirubin already exceeds the phototherapy threshold; waiting another 24 hours risks rapid escalation toward exchange and acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Total bilirubin is well below the exchange threshold of 480 micromol/L and there are no signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; exchange transfusion carries significant procedural risks. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Breastfeeding cessation is not first-line; phototherapy plus continued breastfeeding with lactation support is the AU standard. Cessation undermines establishment and is rarely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

Bilirubin above the phototherapy line at this postnatal age requires admission for intensive phototherapy. Breastfeeding should continue with lactation support and expressed breast milk or formula top-ups to address suboptimal feeding contributing to dehydration and weight loss; DAT and group results guide whether haemolysis is contributing. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; Australian College of Midwives Position Statement)
source_refs: Australian College of Midwives Position Statement

options.rationale: IVIG is indicated for confirmed isoimmune haemolytic disease with rising bilirubin near exchange threshold despite phototherapy, not empirically before serology. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the commonest childhood vasculitis. Most cases are self-limiting with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and microscopic haematuria. Management is supportive analgesia and longitudinal urinalysis plus blood pressure surveillance for 6 months because renal involvement can present late. Steroids are reserved for severe gut pain, orchitis, or proven nephritis. Refer to nephrology for nephrotic-range proteinuria, declining function, or hypertension.
key_points: Steroids do not prevent nephritis - reserve for severe gut, orchitis, biopsy-proven disease
Surveillance for 6 months: weekly urinalysis and BP, then taper
Refer for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine
Most arthralgia and skin disease settles within 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: Urine protein:creatinine ratio over 250 mg/mmol or nephritic syndrome features within 6 months of HSP onset warrants paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy consideration.

options.rationale: Methylprednisolone pulses and biopsy are reserved for nephritic-range proteinuria, declining renal function, or biopsy-proven crescentic disease; this child has mild urinalysis findings only. (Source: KHA-CARI; RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Steroids do not alter the natural history of purpura or prevent renal involvement; they are reserved for severe abdominal pain, orchitis, or established nephritis. Routine prescription overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Antibiotics do not modify the post-infectious vasculitis course; treat any concurrent group A streptococcal pharyngitis on its own merits, not prophylactically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, declining renal function, or persistent significant proteinuria beyond 3 months, not for mild transient urinary changes. (Source: KHA-CARI)

Mild IgA vasculitis with normal blood pressure, normal renal function, and a urine protein:creatinine ratio under 20 mg/mmol is managed conservatively. Ongoing surveillance is essential because nephritis can declare itself up to 6 months after rash onset and dictates referral. Written advice covers when to return (severe abdominal pain, testicular pain, frank haematuria, hypertension). (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura; KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, do not recur within 24 hours, and occur in a child aged 6 months to 6 years with fever from a clear extracranial source. Recurrence happens in around 30%, and the long-term risk of epilepsy is only modestly above background. Investigations, anti-epileptic prophylaxis, and routine antipyretic prophylaxis do not change outcomes. Parental education on positioning, timing, and rescue medication for seizures longer than 5 minutes is the cornerstone of care.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: 6 months to 6 years, generalised, under 15 minutes, no recurrence in 24 hours
No investigations or anti-epileptic prophylaxis - even after recurrence
Parental education and rescue plan for seizures over 5 minutes
Refer if focal features, prolonged, recurrence within 24 hours, or atypical age
explanation.pearls: Rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg is the AU rescue dose if any seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes - this is the prescription on discharge, not daily prophylaxis.

options.rationale: Routine EEG and MRI are not indicated after simple febrile seizures even when recurrent; investigations are reserved for focal, prolonged, or atypical seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

Simple febrile seizures, even recurrent, do not need investigations, anti-epileptic prophylaxis, or routine antipyretic prophylaxis (which does not prevent recurrence). Education on safe positioning, timing the seizure, and rescue rectal diazepam if a seizure exceeds 5 minutes is the AU standard. Long-term epilepsy risk is only modestly increased; reassurance is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Valproate prophylaxis is not used for febrile seizures; the small benefit is outweighed by adverse effects and the natural history is benign in simple cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reduce febrile seizure recurrence; routine alternating dosing risks medication error and adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Fever in children)
Routine neurology referral is unnecessary for simple recurrent febrile seizures; daily rectal diazepam prophylaxis is not evidence-based. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Childhood functional constipation with overflow encopresis is managed in two phases: disimpaction (high-dose macrogol over a few days) and maintenance (daily macrogol with toilet behaviour work). De-shaming the soiling and a structured sit routine after meals reframes the family understanding. Stimulant laxatives are added for refractory cases. Red flags (delayed meconium, ribbon stool from birth, neurological signs, faltering growth) prompt referral for Hirschsprung or other organic disease.
key_points: Disimpaction must precede maintenance laxative use
Oral macrogol with electrolytes is first-line; phosphate enemas avoided
Behavioural sit routine after meals plus de-shaming the soiling is essential
Hirschsprung red flags: delayed meconium, tight rectum, neonatal obstruction
explanation.pearls: Oral macrogol with electrolytes (e.g. Movicol) at the AU paediatric disimpaction schedule clears most impactions within three to five days before transitioning to a maintenance dose.

options.rationale: Hirschsprung typically presents in the first months of life with delayed meconium and a tight rectum on examination; this boy passed meconium normally and has overflow encopresis after age 3 - features against Hirschsprung. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)
Lifestyle measures alone do not clear established faecal impaction; disimpaction is required before maintenance and behavioural work can succeed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Functional constipation with overflow soiling and palpable faecal mass requires disimpaction first. Oral macrogol with electrolytes escalated over three days then continued at maintenance is the AU first-line, paired with a sit routine after meals, a star chart, and de-shaming the soiling. Stimulant laxatives are added if macrogol alone fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
Phosphate enemas risk hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia in children and are not first-line outpatient therapy; oral macrogol is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis without red flags; routine endocrine and coeliac screening is reserved for growth faltering, failure to respond to standard treatment, or other clinical concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionosis of the distal bowel) typically presents in the first 48 hours of life with delayed meconium, abdominal distension, and an explosive rectal squirt after digital examination. A rectosigmoid transition zone is the commonest site; long-segment and total colonic aganglionosis are rarer. Rectal suction biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard, followed by definitive pull-through surgery once enterocolitis is excluded. Enterocolitis (sepsis, severe distension, explosive diarrhoea) is the principal short-term mortality risk and demands rectal washouts, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and decompression.
key_points: Delayed meconium beyond 48 hours plus distension plus squirt sign = suspect Hirschsprung
Rectal suction biopsy is the gold-standard neonatal diagnostic test
Anorectal manometry is unreliable under 1 month; not first-line
Hirschsprung enterocolitis is the principal short-term mortality risk
explanation.pearls: Rectal suction biopsy shows absent ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus with hypertrophied unmyelinated nerve trunks; acetylcholinesterase staining or calretinin loss confirms the diagnosis.

options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease is suspected from delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, the explosive 'squirt sign' after rectal examination, and rectosigmoid transition zone on X-ray. Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks and increased acetylcholinesterase activity is the diagnostic gold standard before staged pull-through. Contrast enema can support but is not diagnostic and can miss ultra-short segment disease. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus; RCH CPG: Neonatal bowel obstruction)

Contrast enema findings of microcolon are characteristic of meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis - not Hirschsprung where a transition zone with proximal dilatation is seen. The string sign is a small bowel pattern, not a Hirschsprung feature. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal bowel obstruction)

Manometry detects the absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex but is technically difficult and unreliable in the neonatal period; suction biopsy is the AU standard in newborns. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus)
Ultrasound does not characterise mural innervation; it cannot diagnose aganglionosis and is not part of the diagnostic algorithm. (Source: ANZAPS Hirschsprung consensus)

Sweat testing assesses cystic fibrosis-related meconium ileus, not Hirschsprung; antenatal scans, no family history, and the squirt sign with rectosigmoid transition point do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: New-onset paediatric type 1 diabetes without acidosis is managed by admission for subcutaneous insulin initiation and structured family education over several days. Acidosis (pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L) defines DKA and triggers a separate fluid and infusion pathway. Diagnosis rests on random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; OGTT is not required when symptomatic. Islet autoantibody and C-peptide testing supports type but does not delay insulin start.
key_points: DKA threshold: pH under 7.3 OR bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L
Symptomatic plus random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes - no OGTT
Subcutaneous basal-bolus initiation in absence of acidosis
Family education during admission is part of the standard pathway
explanation.pearls: Diabetic ketoacidosis fluid replacement in children uses 0.9% sodium chloride at a maintenance rate calculated over 48 hours, never as repeated large boluses, to reduce cerebral oedema risk.

options.rationale: Intravenous fluids and an insulin infusion are reserved for diabetic ketoacidosis (pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 mmol/L) or significant dehydration; this child is normoglycaemic-range for new-onset diabetes without acidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)

New-onset paediatric type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis is admitted for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin initiation, structured family education, and arrangement of outpatient diabetes team follow-up. RCH and APEG protocols use a multi-day inpatient education pathway before discharge. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook; RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

OGTT is unnecessary when a child has classical symptoms and a random glucose over 11.1 mmol/L; outpatient management without insulin risks rapid progression to ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)

Metformin is the first agent for paediatric type 2 diabetes; this child has the type 1 phenotype (rapid weight loss, classical symptoms over weeks) and requires insulin. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Handbook)
Discharge without insulin or formal education is unsafe in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes; vomiting after discharge would already represent decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric asthma is graded mild, moderate, severe, or life-threatening by work of breathing, air entry, oxygen saturation, and conscious state. Severe disease starts with back-to-back salbutamol, oral prednisolone, and oxygen as needed; persistent severity adds nebulised ipratropium to the first three back-to-back doses. Failure to respond escalates to intravenous magnesium sulfate, then aminophylline. Silent chest, exhaustion, or altered conscious state mandates paediatric intensive care escalation.
key_points: Severity grades: mild, moderate, severe, life-threatening
Severe: back-to-back salbutamol plus ipratropium plus oral steroid
Failure of severe pathway: IV magnesium sulfate next
Life-threatening features: silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness
explanation.pearls: Nebulised ipratropium 250 mcg is added to the first three back-to-back salbutamol doses in severe asthma in children under 12, and stopped thereafter to avoid no incremental benefit.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for exhaustion, silent chest, falling oxygen saturation, or altered consciousness; this child remains alert with good air entry and improving tachypnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Severe asthma not fully responsive to initial salbutamol plus oral steroid receives nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 mcg added to the first three back-to-back salbutamol doses; this is the AU paediatric step-up at this severity. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the next escalation if she fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma; National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

options.rationale: Aminophylline is a later step in life-threatening asthma after magnesium has failed; it has a narrow therapeutic window and significant adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Subcutaneous adrenaline is used for anaphylactic bronchospasm or as a temporising measure when inhaled therapy cannot be delivered; nebulised therapy is being delivered effectively here. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

Children requiring continuous bronchodilator and accessory muscle use require ongoing inpatient observation; discharge is unsafe until the salbutamol interval has stretched to at least 3 hours. (Source: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australian Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the commonest hip disorder in adolescents, particularly overweight boys aged 10-15 years. Knee or thigh pain with a limp is the most common presentation; obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the classic examination sign. Diagnosis is by plain pelvis X-ray with frog-lateral views demonstrating slip; MRI detects pre-slip with normal X-rays. Treatment is urgent in-situ percutaneous pinning with strict non-weight-bearing in the interim to prevent acute-on-chronic slip and avascular necrosis.
key_points: SCFE is a paediatric orthopaedic emergency - immediate non-weight-bearing
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the classic sign
Plain pelvis with frog-lateral views is the diagnostic test
Avascular necrosis risk rises with delay and weight-bearing
explanation.pearls: Knee or thigh pain in an adolescent with no clear knee pathology should prompt a hip examination; SCFE can present as referred knee pain without any hip complaint.

sources.label: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position
RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child

options.rationale: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a paediatric orthopaedic emergency. The patient is made non-weight-bearing immediately to reduce the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis, and admitted for urgent in-situ percutaneous pinning. Bilateral prophylactic pinning is considered in selected high-risk patients but the contralateral side is usually monitored. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.rationale: Physiotherapy in active SCFE risks acute-on-chronic progression of the slip; this is a surgical emergency. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.rationale: Diagnosis has been made on plain X-ray with frog-lateral views; MRI is reserved for pre-slip suspicion with normal X-rays. Imaging delay risks progression. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.rationale: Analgesia masks pain that protects against further slip; routine review in a week is unacceptable for an emergency. (Source: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position)
source_refs: AOA Australian Orthopaedic Association SCFE Position

options.rationale: Transient synovitis presents acutely in younger children with a recent viral illness and an irritable hip on examination; the X-ray diagnosis here is SCFE. (Source: RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Limping or non-weight-bearing child

explanation.summary: A brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) replaces the older ALTE term. Low-risk BRUE requires age over 60 days, gestation over 32 weeks with corrected age over 45 weeks, a single brief episode under 1 minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a normal examination. Low-risk BRUE allows discharge after shared decision-making; higher-risk BRUE is observed and selectively investigated. Pertussis testing, ECG, and head imaging are pursued only when targeted features (cough exposure, dysrhythmia clues, focal neurological signs) are present.
key_points: Low-risk BRUE criteria include age over 60 days
Higher-risk: short-stay observation and selective testing
Pertussis PCR if cough exposure or paroxysmal episode
ECG for any suspected arrhythmia or syncope-like features
explanation.pearls: BRUE is by definition unexplained: a clear precipitant (gastro-oesophageal reflux event observed, choking on milk, breath-holding spell) means the event is not a BRUE and is managed on its own pathway.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

options.rationale: This is a low-risk BRUE (age over 60 days when assessed, term, no concerning features, normal examination, single brief episode); panel testing and admission is not part of the low-risk algorithm. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)
This infant is under 60 days of age, which classifies him as a higher-risk BRUE; outright discharge without observation does not meet low-risk criteria. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

Infants under 60 days are not classified as low-risk BRUE even when otherwise reassuring. A period of monitored short-stay observation, capturing repeat events and reviewing feeding, is the AU pathway, with discharge once observation is unremarkable and parental education and safety-netting are documented. (Source: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event; AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

options.rationale: Routine gastroenterology workup is not indicated after an isolated BRUE without recurrent feeding-related events or growth failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief resolved unexplained event

options.rationale: Broad metabolic and imaging panels are reserved for higher-risk BRUEs with concerning features (recurrent events, persistent abnormal examination, family history of metabolic disease). (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Passive antibody neutralises live attenuated viral vaccine virus before it can replicate, so measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines must be separated from immunoglobulin by an interval that scales with the dose given. The Australian Immunisation Handbook sets that interval at about 11 months after intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg, the dose used in Kawasaki disease, compared with three months after anti-D and shorter intervals after small transfusions. Inactivated, conjugate and toxoid vaccines are unaffected and should be given on time so the child does not fall further behind. If a live vaccine is given inside the interval it does not harm the child but should be repeated after the interval has elapsed. In context, Kawasaki disease is treated with a single very large dose of pooled human immunoglobulin, so every child treated for it carries a documented immunisation deferral that the treating team must hand over to the general practitioner.
key_points: Immunoglobulin 2 g/kg defers measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines for about 11 months.
Inactivated, conjugate and toxoid vaccines are given on schedule.
A live vaccine given inside the interval is repeated later, not counted.
The deferral must be written into the discharge summary and the immunisation record.
explanation.pearls: The interval scales with the immunoglobulin dose, so look the product up rather than applying one remembered number to every blood product.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: High-dose immunoglobulin at 2 g/kg blunts the response to live attenuated viral vaccines for about 11 months, so measles-mumps-rubella is deferred that long while inactivated and conjugate vaccines proceed on schedule. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Giving both today would be right after ordinary intramuscular immunoglobulin or a blood product at low dose, where the deferral interval is much shorter or nil. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Blanket deferral would apply if he were receiving ongoing immunosuppression; passive antibody interferes with live viral vaccines only, not with inactivated or conjugate vaccines. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)
Serological confirmation after vaccination is used in specific occupational and outbreak settings, not as a workaround for a known interference interval. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

Three months is the interval after small-volume products such as anti-D or a washed red cell transfusion; 2 g/kg of immunoglobulin sits at the far end of the table. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: PECARN stratifies paediatric blunt head injury into high, intermediate, and low risk. High-risk features mandate CT; low-risk allows discharge. Intermediate risk allows observation versus CT with parental input. In children under 2, an isolated non-frontal scalp haematoma is intermediate. Observation with serial examination spares unnecessary radiation in an at-risk paediatric brain. Children with high-risk features (GCS under 15 at 2 hours, palpable depressed fracture, basal skull fracture signs, non-accidental injury concerns) are imaged.
key_points: PECARN high-risk: GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected depressed or basal skull fracture, NAI
Intermediate-risk under 2: non-frontal scalp haematoma is a positive predictor
Observation with serial examination is acceptable in intermediate risk
CT not MRI for acute decision-making
explanation.pearls: In children under 2, an isolated non-frontal scalp haematoma is an intermediate-risk PECARN feature; a frontal haematoma in an otherwise well child does not elevate risk.

options.rationale: The combination of age under 2 to 3 with a parietal non-frontal scalp haematoma and observed lethargy fails the PECARN low-risk criteria for under-2s and requires observation or imaging. (Source: PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)

Under PECARN intermediate-risk criteria (non-frontal scalp haematoma in under 2, lethargy, single vomit) the choice is between observation and imaging, with parental input. A period of observation with serial GCS, pupil checks, and trend of conscious state is the AU first-line approach in a stable child with no focal signs. CT is the next step if deterioration or persistent symptoms occur. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury; PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)

Immediate CT is reserved for high-risk PECARN features (GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture, suspected non-accidental injury); observation is acceptable for intermediate-risk children. (Source: PECARN Paediatric Head Injury Rule)
Plain skull X-ray has been superseded by clinical decision rules; it neither rules in nor out clinically important traumatic brain injury reliably. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

MRI is the second-line imaging modality for paediatric head injury (typically follow-up) and is impractical acutely without anaesthesia; CT is the acute test where imaging is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

explanation.summary: Australian neonatal pulse oximetry screening detects critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) at 24-48 hours of age, before duct closure typically unmasks duct-dependent lesions. The protocol measures pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) saturation. A fail occurs with either limb under 90%, both limbs under 95% on three readings 1 hour apart, or a persistent pre-post differential of more than 3%. Failed screen mandates urgent echocardiography; prostaglandin E1 is reserved for clinical decompensation pending the result.
key_points: Screen at 24-48 hours of age, before discharge
Fail thresholds: either limb under 90%, both under 95%, or pre-post differential over 3%
Failed screen: urgent echocardiography, not repeat screening
Prostaglandin E1 reserved for clinical decompensation
explanation.pearls: Duct closure in the first week of life unmasks duct-dependent CCHD (HLHS, critical AS, severe coarctation, IAA); the pulse oximetry screen is designed to find these before that catastrophe.

sources.label: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline
RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Persistent pre-post differential under 95% on the AU pulse oximetry algorithm at this stage triggers urgent echocardiography rather than delayed re-screening. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline

options.rationale: The AU pulse oximetry screening algorithm fails when either limb is under 90%, or both limbs under 95%, or a persistent pre-post differential of more than 3%; failure prompts urgent echocardiography to exclude critical congenital heart disease (duct-dependent lesions). Prostaglandin E1 is held in reserve pending the result. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline; RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline
RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Empirical prostaglandin is reserved for clinically unwell duct-dependent neonates; the screen has identified an asymptomatic child for whom prompt echocardiography is the appropriate step. (Source: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Discharge before imaging in a baby with a positive screen is unsafe; duct closure (which usually occurs in the first week) can precipitate decompensation of a duct-dependent lesion. (Source: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health Pulse Oximetry Screening Newborn Guideline

options.rationale: Echocardiography is the definitive imaging step; awaiting blood gas changes delays diagnosis and may miss asymptomatic anatomic disease before deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Critical congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and most common in boys from Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, and South-East Asian backgrounds. Acute haemolysis is triggered by oxidative stress (fava beans, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase, infection). Blood film shows bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies; the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Management removes the trigger and supports with transfusion if symptomatic or haemodynamically compromised. G6PD enzyme assay during the acute haemolysis can be falsely normal because reticulocytes have higher activity; repeat 2-3 months after the episode. A familial G6PD test list and an avoid-list for future medications is essential.
key_points: Oxidative trigger list: fava beans, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase
DAT-negative with bite cells and Heinz bodies
Repeat enzyme assay 2-3 months post-event - acute assay can be falsely normal
Family screening and a written avoid-medication list
explanation.pearls: Methylene blue and rasburicase are both contraindicated in G6PD deficiency despite their utility elsewhere; check G6PD status before either drug in at-risk populations.

options.rationale: Acute G6PD-mediated haemolysis is precipitated by an oxidative trigger (fava beans, sulfonamides such as co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, methylene blue, rasburicase). Removal of the trigger is the foundation; red cell transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia, haemodynamic compromise, or rapid haemoglobin fall. Re-introduce safe antibiotics for the otitis. (Source: HSANZ; RCH CPG: Haemolytic anaemia)

Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is DAT-positive (typically with IgG, with or without complement); this child has DAT-negative haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies, characteristic of G6PD deficiency, not autoimmune disease. (Source: HSANZ)

Splenectomy is considered in hereditary spherocytosis with chronic transfusion need or symptomatic anaemia; G6PD deficiency haemolysis is episodic and trigger-related, and splenectomy is rarely useful. (Source: HSANZ)
Rasburicase is one of the agents that can precipitate severe G6PD haemolysis and should be avoided; this child has a non-malignant haemolytic picture. (Source: AMH)
Methylene blue is also contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it relies on NADPH-dependent reduction and itself precipitates haemolysis. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection (RSV predominant) peaking at age 2-6 months. Australian (RCH) guidance starts oxygen at low-flow nasal prongs 1-2 L/min when SpO2 is under 90% and escalates to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min when low-flow fails after at least 2 hours, with a target SpO2 of 90% or above. Salbutamol, corticosteroids, hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and physiotherapy are not routine. Failure of high-flow nasal cannula prompts paediatric intensive care escalation.
key_points: Low-flow oxygen first at 1-2 L/min; target SpO2 >=90%
Escalate to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min after at least 2 hours of low-flow failure
Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline NOT routine
Failure of HFNC: PICU escalation
explanation.pearls: In bronchiolitis under 12 months the AU SpO2 target is 90% (not 92-94%) - lower targets reduce overtreatment without harm in well-perfused infants.

options.rationale: Low-flow oxygen has reached its ceiling and has not improved work of breathing or feeding; the AU bronchiolitis pathway escalates after failure rather than waiting further. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

RCH bronchiolitis guidance escalates to high-flow nasal cannula after failure of low-flow oxygen, defined as ongoing increased work of breathing, feeding compromise, or rising pCO2 despite 1-2 L/min for at least 2 hours. The saturation target is 90% or above (not 92-94%) and the flow is set at 2 L/kg/min. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial)
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis under 12 months; trials have not shown a length-of-stay benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)
Corticosteroids do not improve bronchiolitis outcomes in this age group; chest physiotherapy is similarly not routine. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

A pCO2 of 50 mmHg with a near-normal pH does not by itself mandate intubation; high-flow nasal cannula is the next escalation before invasive ventilation in stable bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral upper-airway infection typically in children aged 6 months to 6 years. The Westley score (5 components - level of consciousness, cyanosis, stridor, air entry, retraction) grades mild (under 3), moderate (3-5), severe (6-11), and impending failure (12 or above). Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is given for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe disease. Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose) is added in severe disease and any child is observed for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild/moderate; 0.6 mg/kg for severe
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (flat dose)
Observation at least 3 hours after last adrenaline
Westley score >=6 = severe
explanation.pearls: Nebulised adrenaline is a temporising measure; without concurrent dexamethasone the stridor can rebound within 2-3 hours.

options.rationale: Mild and moderate croup are treated with dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, but severe croup with stridor at rest requires a higher dose (0.6 mg/kg) and concurrent nebulised adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Severe croup (Westley score 6 or above, stridor at rest with marked recession) receives concurrent nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (a flat dose, not weight-based) and dexamethasone at the higher 0.6 mg/kg oral dose. Children are observed for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Intubation is reserved for severe croup that fails nebulised adrenaline and steroids or shows exhaustion, altered consciousness, or cyanosis; first-line pharmacological treatment has not yet been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral dexamethasone cannot be given, but is not first-line and does not replace adrenaline in severe disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Severe croup with stridor at rest requires pharmacological treatment and at least 3 hours of monitored observation; discharge before adrenaline trial is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Australian (RCH) paediatric UTI guidance reserves renal tract ultrasound for atypical UTI (poor antibiotic response within 48 hours, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine) or recurrent UTI. Infants under 6 months also receive imaging where no antenatal ultrasound coverage has been documented. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and are not part of the RCH cascade. Single typical UTI in a child over 6 months with rapid response does not need routine imaging. The intravenous antibiotic course continues until clinical response and culture sensitivities guide the oral switch.
key_points: Ultrasound during admission for atypical UTI or under 6 months without antenatal imaging
Atypical features include non-E coli, poor 48-hour response, sepsis
DMSA and MCUG NOT in the RCH cascade
Single typical UTI over 6 months does not need routine imaging
explanation.pearls: Recurrent UTI (two or more upper UTIs, or one upper plus one or more lower) triggers ultrasound regardless of age; DMSA still has no place in the RCH algorithm.

options.rationale: This child has atypical UTI features (under 6 months of age, non-E coli pathogen, poor response within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, no antenatal renal ultrasound documentation). RCH guidance triggers a renal tract ultrasound during the current admission for atypical UTI. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is a NICE-derived investigation and is not part of the RCH AU UTI imaging cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Oral switch before clinical response and before imaging risks missing structural abnormality; prophylaxis alone is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
