Surgery is reserved for failed enema reduction, peritonitis, shock, or evidence of perforation; first-line is non-operative enema reduction in stable children. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Colonoscopy has no role in acute intussusception diagnosis or reduction; ultrasound confirms diagnosis and enema reduces. Delay risks bowel necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Oral rehydration delays definitive reduction in confirmed intussusception; without enema or surgical reduction the obstruction progresses to ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents at 3-6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry feeds, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound confirms with pyloric muscle thickness >=3-4 mm and length >=14-17 mm. Pyloromyotomy is curative but is NEVER an emergency; electrolyte correction first, with chloride >100, bicarbonate <30, and urine output established, prevents post-operative apnoea from persistent alkalosis blunting respiratory drive.
key_points: Diagnostic ultrasound criteria: pyloric muscle thickness >=3-4 mm, length >=14-17 mm.
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is the classic biochemistry.
Correct fluid/electrolytes BEFORE surgery to prevent post-op apnoea.
Target chloride >100 mmol/L and bicarbonate <30 mmol/L before theatre.
Erythromycin in early infancy is itself a risk factor for pyloric stenosis.
explanation.pearls: Pyloric stenosis is a medical preparation, then a surgical fix - never a 1am operation. Chloride >100 and bicarbonate <30 are the gates.

options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is never a surgical emergency; operating on a child with hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis risks post-operative apnoea from persistent metabolic alkalosis depressing respiratory drive. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Correction of hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis to chloride >100 and bicarbonate <30 with adequate urine output is the RCH and AAP criteria before pyloromyotomy to prevent post-operative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)
Mechanical gastric outlet obstruction will not respond to thickening; ongoing vomiting will worsen dehydration and alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

Erythromycin has no role in pyloric stenosis (a fixed muscle hypertrophy); surgical pyloromyotomy is curative. Erythromycin in infants is also associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

Ultrasound has already confirmed pyloric stenosis (muscle thickness >=3-4 mm, length >=14-17 mm); contrast study is unnecessary and delays correction of electrolytes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is plotted against age-in-hours on the RCH bilirubin nomogram; the threshold for phototherapy is a function of age, gestation, and risk factors (haemolysis, sepsis, prematurity). A negative DAT and matched maternal-infant ABO blood groups exclude haemolytic disease; this infant has breastfeeding-associated jaundice from inadequate feeding and weight loss, but the bilirubin level itself dictates phototherapy. Continued breastfeeding with lactation support is the standard adjunct rather than formula switching.
key_points: Treatment threshold depends on age in hours plotted on the RCH nomogram.
Negative DAT plus normal reticulocytes excludes immune haemolysis.
Breastfeeding-associated jaundice from inadequate intake is treated with phototherapy plus continued breastfeeding and lactation support.
Exchange transfusion threshold is approximately 425 micromol/L at this age in low-risk infants.
Phototherapy is intensive (multiple lights, maximised skin exposure) when above treatment line.
explanation.pearls: When DAT is negative and ABO/Rh are matched, haemolytic disease is excluded - but the absolute bilirubin level on the RCH nomogram is what determines whether phototherapy starts now, not the underlying mechanism.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: The serum bilirubin of 332 micromol/L at 108 hours of life crosses the RCH phototherapy line for a term infant without risk factors; deferring treatment risks ongoing rise and acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Brief formula supplementation can be considered as an adjunct in dehydration-related jaundice but is not the primary treatment when bilirubin crosses the phototherapy line; phototherapy is required regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Bilirubin 332 micromol/L at 108 hours in a well term infant without haemolysis exceeds the RCH phototherapy threshold; intensive phototherapy with continued breastfeeding plus lactation support is the AU standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Exchange transfusion threshold at 108 hours in a low-risk term infant is approximately >425 micromol/L, or failure of intensive phototherapy; this infant has not reached that line. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Workup for prolonged or pathological jaundice (conjugated, age >14 days, or rising after phototherapy) does not replace immediate phototherapy when the unconjugated bilirubin threshold is crossed. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: RCH guidance on paediatric UTI imaging is more parsimonious than NICE. Renal tract ultrasound is recommended for: any infant <6 months after first UTI, atypical UTI at any age (poor response to 48h antibiotics, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine), and recurrent UTI at any age. MCUG and DMSA are NOT part of the routine RCH cascade - they are reserved for ultrasound abnormalities or selected high-risk infants. This infant is <6 months AND has recurrent UTI, so ultrasound is doubly indicated.
key_points: RCH first-line imaging in recurrent UTI is renal tract ultrasound.
MCUG and DMSA are not in the RCH routine cascade.
Infants <6 months get ultrasound after first UTI regardless of recurrence.
Ultrasound during current illness picks up acute changes (pyonephrosis).
Prophylactic antibiotics in infants are controversial; not routine without anatomy abnormality.
explanation.pearls: RCH UTI cascade: ultrasound is the universal first step in <6 months or recurrent or atypical UTI; do NOT default to DMSA or MCUG based on NICE-derived habits.

options.rationale: MCUG is not in the RCH first-line cascade; it is invasive and reserved for selected cases (abnormal ultrasound, family history, very young child with severe recurrent atypical UTI) after ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
DMSA is not in the RCH cascade and is a NICE construct; AU practice does not routinely screen for scarring after UTI in well children. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
CT KUB is rarely indicated in paediatric UTI workup due to radiation exposure and low yield in well infants without stone risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Per RCH, renal tract ultrasound is the first-line imaging in any infant <6 months with UTI (and in recurrent or atypical UTI at any age); during current illness it picks up acute pyonephrosis, hydronephrosis, and anatomical anomalies. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
Surveillance alone misses correctable anatomical drivers; RCH mandates ultrasound after recurrent UTI in any child and after first UTI in infants <6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: HSP (IgA vasculitis) is the commonest small-vessel vasculitis of childhood and presents with palpable purpura on dependent areas, abdominal pain, arthritis (usually ankles or knees), and renal involvement in 30-50%. The cutaneous and joint disease is self-limiting; renal involvement is the major prognostic determinant. Monitoring strategy: weekly urine dipstick and BP for 6 months minimum; closer surveillance and nephrology referral if PCR rises, macroscopic haematuria persists, or hypertension develops. Steroids do not prevent nephritis but may help abdominal pain.
key_points: HSP: palpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthritis +/- nephritis.
Renal involvement in 30-50%; chief determinant of long-term prognosis.
Monitor urine dipstick and BP weekly for first 6 weeks, then monthly.
Steroids do not prevent nephritis (Cochrane); reserved for severe abdominal pain.
Nephrology referral for nephrotic range proteinuria, declining function, persistent macroscopic haematuria or hypertension.
explanation.pearls: HSP nephritis surveillance is dipstick and BP for at least 6 months - oral prednisolone does NOT prevent progression and is reserved for severe abdominal pain or proven severe nephritis.

options.rationale: Routine corticosteroids do NOT prevent or reduce HSP nephritis progression per Cochrane and KHA-CARI; they may shorten abdominal pain but are not first-line for renal involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Pulse steroids and biopsy are reserved for severe nephritis: nephrotic-range proteinuria, declining renal function, or persistent macroscopic haematuria after 4 weeks; not first-line in moderate proteinuria with normal renal function. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
IVIG has no proven role in HSP and is not in any AU first-line guideline; cost and risks are unjustified. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Visible macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria 2+, and PCR 180 mandate closer monitoring than weekly GP review; missed progression risks end-stage renal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Per RCH, children with HSP and significant renal involvement (PCR >100, persistent macroscopic haematuria, hypertension, declining function) require BP and renal monitoring, with nephrology input if features persist beyond a week. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis affecting children under 5, defined by fever >=4 days plus 4 of 5 of: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, mucositis (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), polymorphous rash, peripheral changes (oedema, desquamation), and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm. Without treatment, coronary artery aneurysms develop in approximately 25%; IVIG 2 g/kg given within 10 days of illness onset reduces this to <5%. Aspirin (high-dose anti-inflammatory then low-dose antiplatelet) is added. Echo at baseline and serial intervals (2, 6 weeks) monitors coronary involvement.
key_points: Diagnosis: fever >=4 days plus 4 of 5 of CRASH-and-burn features.
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within day 10 reduces aneurysms 25% to <5%.
Aspirin: high dose (30-50 mg/kg/day) while febrile, then 3-5 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks.
Echo at baseline, 2 weeks, 6 weeks; sooner if features of coronary involvement.
Incomplete/atypical KD in infants is a high-risk subtype - low threshold for IVIG.
explanation.pearls: IVIG within day 10 of Kawasaki cuts coronary aneurysm rate from 25% to under 5% - the diagnostic threshold of 4 out of 5 features alongside fever justifies treating empirically without awaiting echo.

options.rationale: He meets clinical criteria for Kawasaki disease (fever >=4 days plus 4 of 5 features); IVIG within day 10 of illness reduces coronary aneurysm rate from 25% to 4%; baseline echo guides ongoing monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Low-dose aspirin without IVIG fails to reduce coronary aneurysm risk; delay past day 10 substantially increases aneurysm rate and morbidity. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

Kawasaki disease clinical features (5+ days fever, mucocutaneous changes, peripheral changes, sterile pyuria) differ from staphylococcal/streptococcal illness; antibiotics do not address the vasculitis or aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Treatment is not contingent on echo; baseline echo informs follow-up but IVIG must not be delayed when clinical criteria are met within the 10-day window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
Discharge without IVIG misses the critical treatment window and risks coronary aneurysms; he meets full clinical Kawasaki criteria today. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal disease in a shocked child mandates the AU paediatric sepsis pathway: IV or intraosseous access within 90 seconds (2 failed peripheral attempts triggers IO), blood cultures, first dose of IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg) within the hour, 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus over 5-10 minutes repeatable to 60 mL/kg, and activation of paediatric retrieval. Lumbar puncture is deferred until shock is corrected and there are no signs of raised ICP. Inotropes (adrenaline) are added after fluids if shock persists. Household contacts require post-exposure ciprofloxacin or rifampicin.
key_points: Time-to-antibiotic in meningococcal sepsis is outcome-determining.
IO access after 2 failed IV attempts or 90 seconds.
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV is the AU empirical agent.
Defer LP in shock or raised ICP signs.
Notify Public Health and arrange contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin).
explanation.pearls: Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV/IO within the hour beats every other intervention in meningococcal sepsis - never delay it for LP or further imaging.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics in fulminant meningococcaemia are inadequate; IV access (or IO if 2 attempts fail) with immediate IV third-generation cephalosporin is the AU standard before retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

Empirical IV ceftriaxone within the first hour, IV/IO access, fluid resuscitation, and retrieval activation is the AU paediatric sepsis pathway; do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture in shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: LP is contraindicated in shock or raised ICP; antibiotics must not be delayed for LP. Blood cultures + PCR can identify Neisseria meningitidis post-antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

Dexamethasone is given for suspected pneumococcal or Hib meningitis with antibiotics but does not improve outcomes in meningococcal sepsis and should not delay the first antibiotic dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)
Mortality in meningococcal sepsis rises with every hour of antibiotic delay; observation is not appropriate when shock signs are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

explanation.summary: Bacterial tracheitis presents as croup that does not improve with steroids and nebulised adrenaline, with the child becoming high-fever and toxic-appearing; tracheal tenderness is a classic distinguishing sign. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism. The airway is at high risk of obstruction by pseudomembranous tracheal debris. Management is ENT and anaesthetic-led airway evaluation in theatre (typically intubation under inhalational induction with backup tracheostomy plan), tracheal toilet of debris, and empirical IV antibiotics covering S aureus and H influenzae (flucloxacillin plus cefotaxime). Discriminate from epiglottitis (drooling, tripod, soft stridor without tracheal tenderness).
key_points: Bacterial tracheitis: croup not responding to steroid + adrenaline, plus toxic appearance.
Tracheal tenderness on palpation helps distinguish it from croup.
Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus.
Theatre-based airway evaluation by ENT and anaesthetist with intubation.
Antibiotics: flucloxacillin plus cefotaxime IV.
explanation.pearls: When croup fails two doses of adrenaline plus dexamethasone in a toxic febrile child, escalate to theatre for intubation and start flucloxacillin plus cefotaxime IV - bacterial tracheitis kills airways within hours of misdiagnosis as refractory croup.

options.rationale: Failure of two doses of adrenaline plus dexamethasone in toxic-appearing high-fever child with tracheal tenderness signals bacterial tracheitis, not refractory croup; ongoing observation risks airway loss. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Lateral neck X-ray in a toxic child with stridor is dangerous (can precipitate airway obstruction) and delays definitive airway evaluation; imaging is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Bacterial tracheitis (high fever, toxic appearance, tracheal tenderness, failed croup treatment) is an airway emergency; theatre-based evaluation with intubation and empirical S aureus + H influenzae cover is the AU standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Heliox and HFNC do not treat the underlying pseudomembranous bacterial airway disease; definitive airway management and IV antibiotics are required, not non-invasive ventilation alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Amoxicillin alone misses S aureus (most common in bacterial tracheitis) and delays definitive airway management; combined flucloxacillin and cefotaxime is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Foreign body aspiration in toddlers presents with a witnessed choking event followed by lateralised signs (decreased breath sounds, wheeze on one side) and air-trapping on expiratory CXR (hyperinflation, mediastinal shift). Peanuts are the most common organic foreign body in Australia and cause chemical bronchitis if retained. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in theatre is the AU standard for both diagnosis and definitive removal. Postural physiotherapy may convert partial to complete obstruction and is contraindicated. Plain CXR may be normal in 30% of cases - history and exam guide the decision to scope, not imaging.
key_points: Toddler + choking history + lateralised signs = aspirated foreign body until proven otherwise.
Expiratory CXR shows hyperinflation on side of obstruction; inspiratory may be normal.
Rigid bronchoscopy under GA in theatre is the AU standard for removal.
Postural physiotherapy is contraindicated; risk of converting partial to complete obstruction.
Peanuts cause chemical bronchitis; remove urgently.
explanation.pearls: A normal CXR does not exclude foreign body aspiration in a toddler with a clear choking history and lateralised signs - rigid bronchoscopy under GA both diagnoses and treats.

options.rationale: Foreign body aspiration with classic history and lateralised signs does not respond to bronchodilators; the obstruction is mechanical and requires removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration)

Postural physiotherapy may dislodge a peripheral object into a more proximal airway causing complete obstruction; it is contraindicated as a removal strategy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration)

Flexible bronchoscopy can be diagnostic but is suboptimal for retrieval of nuts (granulating, friable). Rigid bronchoscopy in theatre under GA is the AU standard for both diagnosis and removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration)

Classic aspiration history, lateralised auscultation signs, and CXR hyperinflation with mediastinal shift mandate rigid bronchoscopy under GA in theatre; peanuts particularly cause chemical bronchitis if retained. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration)

Discharge risks progressive obstruction, post-obstructive pneumonia, and chronic suppurative damage from retained organic foreign body; removal is time-sensitive. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body aspiration)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency with a 6 hour window for testicular salvage. Classic features (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex) should prompt direct theatre without Doppler delay. Bilateral orchidopexy is performed even if the contralateral testis appears normal because the anatomical predisposition (bell-clapper deformity) is bilateral. Differential includes epididymo-orchitis (gradual onset, fever, urinary symptoms, normal cremasteric, pyuria) and torsion of the appendix testis (gradual onset, blue dot sign). Imaging may be reserved for atypical presentations only.
key_points: Salvage rate ~90% under 6 hours; drops to ~50% by 12 hours and near zero by 24 hours.
Direct theatre without Doppler for classic clinical presentation.
Bilateral orchidopexy because bell-clapper is bilateral.
Absent cremasteric reflex has high sensitivity (about 99%).
Manual detorsion (rotate medial to lateral, book opening) only if theatre delay >1 hour.
explanation.pearls: Classic torsion does not need Doppler - the 6 hour clock is more sensitive than imaging. Bilateral orchidopexy is mandatory because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute scrotum guidance

options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound has high false negative rates and delays theatre; clinical diagnosis is sufficient to proceed direct to scrotal exploration in classic presentation within the 6 hour window. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)
Manual detorsion is a temporising measure when surgery is delayed, not a substitute for definitive exploration and bilateral orchidopexy. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

Epididymo-orchitis is unlikely without urinary symptoms, no urethral discharge, no fever, in a 14-year-old with sudden onset pain; missing torsion in the 6 hour window costs the testis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)
Discharge in suspected testicular torsion is negligent; salvage rate drops sharply after 6 hours of ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

Classic torsion (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex) within 5 hours requires immediate theatre; salvage rate approximately 90% under 6 hours, then falls sharply. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus follows a time-based algorithm: first benzodiazepine (buccal/IM midazolam, IV lorazepam, or IV diazepam) at 5-10 minutes, second benzodiazepine if still seizing at 10-15 minutes, second-line agent (levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate) at 15-25 minutes, and intubation with thiopentone infusion in PICU for refractory status >30 minutes. IM midazolam is a reliable second benzodiazepine when IV access is delayed. ESETT (2019) showed levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproate are equivalent as second-line agents. Always check glucose, electrolytes, and consider underlying cause once seizure is controlled.
key_points: Time-based algorithm: 1st benzo 5 min, 2nd benzo 10-15 min, 2nd line 15-25 min.
IM midazolam reliable when IV access is delayed.
ESETT: levetiracetam, phenytoin, valproate equivalent for second-line.
Intubation with thiopentone for refractory status >30 minutes.
Check glucose first; treat hypoglycaemia (2 mL/kg 10% dextrose).
explanation.pearls: A second benzodiazepine dose precedes the second-line agent in the APLS Australia algorithm - jumping straight to phenytoin or levetiracetam at 12 minutes is non-standard.

options.rationale: Second benzodiazepine dose is appropriate at 10 minutes if first dose ineffective and IV access not yet obtained; IM midazolam absorbs reliably; second-line agent (levetiracetam or phenytoin) follows at 15-20 minutes. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

Phenytoin is a valid second-line agent but should follow a second benzodiazepine dose; jumping straight to phenytoin without a second benzo is not the AU APLS pathway. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

Levetiracetam is a valid alternative second-line but should follow a second benzodiazepine; ESETT trial shows levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproate are all equivalent second-line agents but second benzo precedes them. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)
Intubation and thiopentone are reserved for refractory status (>30 minutes despite first and second line); current step is second benzo. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

Imaging is appropriate after the seizure is controlled and the airway secured; pursuing imaging before stopping the seizure prolongs ictal injury. (Source: APLS Australia Algorithm: Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Intraosseous access is the recommended next step after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in a critically ill child requiring resuscitation. Proximal tibia (1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity on medial flat surface) is the standard paediatric site, with proximal humerus and distal femur as alternatives. IO can deliver all fluids and drugs (including adrenaline, bicarbonate, blood products), and blood can be drawn for cultures and gases. EZ-IO power driver is the AU standard device. IO should be replaced by definitive IV/central access within 24 hours due to risk of osteomyelitis if used longer.
key_points: IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in resuscitation.
Proximal tibia: 1-2 cm below tibial tuberosity, medial flat surface.
All fluids and drugs can be given via IO; blood samples can be drawn.
Replace with definitive access within 24 hours.
Avoid in fractured bone or recent IO attempt in same bone.
explanation.pearls: EZ-IO power-driven proximal tibia takes under 60 seconds and accepts every resuscitation drug - waiting for the retrieval team or doing a cut-down only delays access.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: APLS Australia and RCH paediatric sepsis pathway mandate IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds in shocked children; further peripheral attempts delay resuscitation. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

AU APLS and RCH sepsis pathway mandate IO insertion after 2 failed peripheral attempts or 90 seconds; proximal tibia is the standard paediatric site; IO can deliver all fluids, drugs and bloods can be drawn. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)
Waiting 30 minutes for retrieval risks death from untreated septic shock; IO can be inserted in <60 seconds by any APLS-trained clinician. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)
Venous cut-down is slower, requires surgical skill, and has largely been replaced by IO insertion in paediatric resuscitation; it is not first-line in 2026. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)
Subcutaneous fluids have no role in shock resuscitation; absorption is too slow. (Source: APLS Australia: Vascular access)

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is a toxin-mediated illness presenting with fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma, multi-organ dysfunction and (later) desquamation. Menstrual TSS is associated with prolonged tampon use; non-menstrual TSS with surgical/burn wounds or skin abscesses. Management has three pillars: (1) organism eradication with flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA suspected), (2) toxin suppression with clindamycin (binds ribosome inhibiting exotoxin synthesis), and (3) source control (tampon removal, wound debridement). IVIG 1-2 g/kg is considered for refractory shock to neutralise circulating superantigen. Streptococcal TSS is the differential and is treated similarly (penicillin + clindamycin).
key_points: Three pillars: anti-staphylococcal antibiotic + clindamycin (toxin suppression) + source control.
Clindamycin binds ribosome to inhibit exotoxin synthesis - critical adjunct.
Tampon removal is immediate source control in menstrual TSS.
IVIG 1-2 g/kg for refractory shock to neutralise superantigen.
Differential streptococcal TSS treated with penicillin + clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin within the first hour suppresses ongoing toxin production at the ribosome - flucloxacillin alone kills the organism but does not switch off the exotoxin already being made.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome
RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.rationale: Vancomycin alone does not suppress toxin production; clindamycin is added specifically to inhibit ribosomal toxin synthesis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole covers intra-abdominal sepsis, not staphylococcal TSS; source control by tampon removal is the first priority in menstrual TSS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.rationale: Menstrual TSS is staphylococcal toxin-mediated; flucloxacillin treats organism, clindamycin suppresses toxin synthesis at the ribosome, tampon removal is source control, IVIG neutralises circulating toxin in severe cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is broad-spectrum but inferior anti-staphylococcal activity to flucloxacillin and does not suppress toxin; delayed source control increases ongoing toxin release. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

options.rationale: Oral therapy in shocked patient is inappropriate; gentamicin lacks anti-staphylococcal toxin suppression activity; doxycycline is not adequate monotherapy in fulminant TSS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Toxic shock syndrome

explanation.summary: Exertional heatstroke in young athletes is defined by core temperature >40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction in the context of exertion. Cold water immersion (CWI) at 2-15 °C is the fastest cooling method (rate 0.15-0.2 °C/min) and is associated with the lowest mortality when applied within 30 minutes of collapse. The target is to cool TO 39 °C within 30 minutes - not lower - to avoid overshoot hypothermia. Evaporative cooling is an acceptable alternative when CWI is not feasible. Complications include rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000), AKI, DIC, hepatic injury, and arrhythmias - resuscitation with IV crystalloid and electrolyte correction proceeds concurrently. Paracetamol and dantrolene do NOT have a role.
key_points: Cold water immersion is first-line for exertional heatstroke; cooling rate ~0.2 °C/min.
Target cool to 39 °C within 30 minutes; avoid overshoot to hypothermia.
Evaporative cooling is acceptable when CWI unavailable but slower.
Paracetamol has no role in exertional hyperthermia (no pyrogen).
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000), AKI, DIC, hepatic injury.
explanation.pearls: Cold water immersion cools at 0.2 °C per minute - target 39 °C then stop, because overshoot hypothermia kills as readily as the original hyperthermia.

options.rationale: Tepid sponging is too slow for exertional heatstroke with core >40 °C; paracetamol does not lower temperature in non-pyrogen-mediated hyperthermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

Evaporative cooling is acceptable when CWI is unavailable but is slower (cooling rate 0.05 vs 0.2 °C/min) and inferior to CWI for exertional heatstroke; paracetamol is ineffective. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

Endovascular cooling has slower cooling rate than CWI, requires expertise and equipment usually unavailable in ED, and is reserved for ICU when other methods fail. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

Cold water immersion (2-15 °C) targeting cool-to-39 °C within 30 minutes is the most rapid cooling method (rate 0.2 °C/min) and has the lowest mortality in exertional heatstroke; stopping at 39 °C avoids overshoot to hypothermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

Ice packs at major vessels are slower than CWI (cooling rate 0.03 °C/min) and inferior for exertional heatstroke; targeting 36 °C risks overshoot to hypothermia. (Source: Sports Medicine Australia: Heat illness)

explanation.summary: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula presents in the neonate with the classic triad of frothy oral secretions, choking/coughing/cyanosis with first feeds, and inability to pass an orogastric tube. Antenatal polyhydramnios (from inability to swallow amniotic fluid) is suggestive. The most common type (85%) is oesophageal atresia with distal TOF (Gross type C) - identified by OGT coiling in upper pouch at 10-12 cm with gas-filled stomach on plain abdominal film (gas reaches stomach via the distal fistula). Pure oesophageal atresia (no fistula) shows OGT coiling AND a gasless abdomen. Contrast studies are contraindicated due to aspiration into the lungs causing chemical pneumonitis. Look for VACTERL associations (Vertebral, Anorectal, Cardiac, TE, Renal, Limb). Definitive management is paediatric surgical repair.
key_points: Triad: frothy oral secretions, choking with first feeds, OGT cannot pass.
Antenatal polyhydramnios is suggestive.
OGT coiling at 10-12 cm + gas in stomach on CXR = Gross type C (85%).
Contrast swallow CONTRAINDICATED (aspiration risk).
Screen for VACTERL associations: vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, limb.
explanation.pearls: OGT plus a plain chest-and-abdomen X-ray confirms TOF in under 10 minutes - never order a barium swallow in a neonate with frothy oral secretions, the contrast will spill into the lungs.

options.rationale: Thickened formula in tracheo-oesophageal fistula risks ongoing aspiration; the clinical picture (frothy oral secretions, choking with feed, scaphoid abdomen with polyhydramnios) demands urgent workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
Suspected TOF cannot be discharged; failure to recognise leads to repeated aspiration, pneumonia, and abdominal distension from gas via fistula. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
Echo is part of VACTERL workup but does not diagnose TOF; passage of orogastric tube with chest and abdomen X-ray is the immediate confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

Contrast swallow is CONTRAINDICATED in suspected TOF due to aspiration into lungs causing chemical pneumonitis; OGT + plain film is the safe diagnostic approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

OGT passage with coiling at 10-12 cm plus gas-filled stomach on plain X-ray confirms oesophageal atresia with distal TOF (most common type); contrast study is contraindicated due to aspiration risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Tracheo-oesophageal fistula)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway escalates respiratory support in steps: room air, then low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min for infants), then high-flow nasal cannula (2 L/kg/min heated humidified) on the ward, then non-invasive ventilation in PICU. The SpO2 target is 90% or above on minimal support. Bronchodilators, nebulised hypertonic saline, systemic corticosteroids, and routine chest physiotherapy are not recommended for bronchiolitis. Apnoeas, exhaustion, or rising pCO2 are PICU-level triggers.
key_points: SpO2 target is 90% (not 92-94%) in bronchiolitis under RCH
Low-flow oxygen via nasal prongs is capped at 2 L/min in infants
HFNC 2 L/kg/min is the standard ward-level escalation step
Bronchodilators have no role in bronchiolitis under 12 months
Apnoeas, rising pCO2, or HFNC failure trigger PICU transfer
explanation.pearls: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen flow rate in infants is 2 L/min maximum; if persistent SpO2 under 90% or moderate work of breathing after 2 hours, escalate to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min.

options.rationale: RCH defines low-flow failure as ongoing moderate work of breathing or SpO2 below 90% after 2 hours on maximal low-flow; HFNC at 2 L/kg/min is the next step in escalation in the ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Standard nasal prongs deliver up to 2 L/min in infants under 12 months per RCH; flows above this are uncomfortable, dry the airway, and are not part of the bronchiolitis escalation pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

After 2 hours on low-flow with persistent saturations below the 90% target and ongoing moderate work of breathing, continuing the same therapy meets the RCH definition of low-flow failure and risks delayed escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months and do not change outcomes or oxygen requirement; the wheeze reflects small-airway plugging, not bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

BiPAP bypasses the HFNC step in the RCH escalation ladder; HFNC failure (rising pCO2, rising RR despite 2 L/kg/min, exhaustion) is the trigger to escalate to non-invasive ventilation in PICU. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: ASCIA and RCH use weight bands for IM adrenaline in paediatric anaphylaxis to remove calculation error in resuscitation: 7.5-20 kg (under 5 years) 150 mcg, 20 kg and over 300 mcg, 50 kg and over 500 mcg. The IM site is the anterolateral mid-thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if no response. IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases after 2 IM doses with cardiac monitoring.
key_points: ASCIA paediatric IM adrenaline uses banded doses, not per-kg arithmetic
7.5-20 kg child receives 150 mcg IM (EpiPen Jr equivalent)
Anterolateral mid-thigh is the only IM site
Repeat at 5 minute intervals if persistent symptoms
IV adrenaline only after 2 failed IM doses with cardiac monitoring
explanation.pearls: 150 mcg IM adrenaline is the ASCIA dose for any child 7.5-20 kg; the banded table is the AU standard precisely because resuscitation is not the moment for mg/kg arithmetic.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Calculating 10 mcg/kg arithmetic from a non-current weight is the historical method that ASCIA replaced; the per-kg formula is no longer the preferred prescribing approach in the emergency setting. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after at least 2 IM doses and only with cardiac monitoring; first-line is always IM into the anterolateral thigh. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: 300 mcg (EpiPen) is the ASCIA banded dose for children 20 kg or more (approximately 6 years and older), not for an 11 kg toddler; overdose risks tachyarrhythmia in small children. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: The ASCIA banded table assigns 150 mcg IM adrenaline to children in the 7.5-20 kg band (under 5 years), independent of exact weight; matches an EpiPen Jr. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline can supplement upper airway oedema management AFTER IM adrenaline; it does not address systemic anaphylaxis and is never the first single best initial intervention. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric practice prefers NGT rehydration over IV for moderate dehydration without shock because it is faster to start, less invasive, has fewer complications, and matches outcomes of IV therapy. A single dose of oral ondansetron (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg) is recommended for vomiting; repeat doses are not. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure, decreased conscious state, or significant electrolyte/acid-base derangement. Routine stool studies and antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first-line for moderate dehydration without shock
Ondansetron is single-dose only: 2 mg (8-15 kg) or 4 mg (15-30 kg)
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure
Routine stool studies do not change acute management
Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: NGT ORS at 25 mL/kg over the first hour is the RCH protocol for moderate dehydration after failed oral intake; IV access is needed only if NGT fails or shock develops.

options.rationale: Discharge home is inappropriate when oral intake has just failed in the department with a documented 5.5% weight loss and ongoing vomiting after ondansetron. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, NGT failure, or significant electrolyte derangement; NGT is preferred for moderate dehydration with normal electrolytes and no shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

RCH first-line for moderate dehydration after failed oral intake is NGT rehydration with ORS; faster, safer, and equally effective as IV in moderate dehydration without shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Ondansetron is a single dose only in paediatric gastroenteritis and the dose for 8-15 kg is 2 mg; repeated dosing is not recommended and delays definitive rehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Stool studies are not routine in uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis and do not change acute management; rehydration is the priority and is not stool-result dependent. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is the rule in infants and a leading cause of acquired coronary artery disease in children. AHA/RCH supplementary laboratory criteria (CRP over 30 mg/L plus 3 of: anaemia for age, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30 g/L, ALT elevation, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria) support empirical IVIG when fewer than 4 of 5 classical features are present. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be given within 10 days of fever onset. Steroids are adjunctive in IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk infants; echocardiography is performed to baseline coronary status but does not gate initial treatment.
key_points: Treat incomplete Kawasaki on supportive lab criteria, do not wait for echo
IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk to about 5%
Infants under 12 months have the highest aneurysm risk
Sterile pyuria, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytosis are supportive
Pulse steroids are adjunctive (Kobayashi-high or IVIG-resistant), not primary
explanation.pearls: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within day 10 of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm risk from around 25% to under 5%; infants under 12 months should be treated on lower thresholds because incomplete presentation is the norm.

sources.label: AHA 2017 Scientific Statement Diagnosis Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

options.rationale: Treatment of suspected Kawasaki disease is not contingent on a coronary abnormality; delaying IVIG beyond day 10 of illness markedly increases the risk of coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Infants under 12 months are at highest risk of coronary aneurysms and most often present with incomplete criteria; AHA and RCH explicitly recommend treating incomplete Kawasaki on supportive laboratory features. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Incomplete Kawasaki in an infant with 3 of 5 criteria plus elevated CRP, transaminitis, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia and thrombocytosis meets RCH IVIG criteria; treat within 10 days of fever onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Persistent fever for 7 days with documented sterile pyuria, no localising focus, and Kawasaki features makes broadened antibiotics inappropriate as a primary intervention; the diagnosis is Kawasaki until proven otherwise. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

Pulse steroids are reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease or selected high-risk cases (Kobayashi score, infants under 12 months may be considered for adjunctive steroid); they are NOT primary monotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Paediatric febrile neutropenia (single tympanic temperature 38.5 °C or above OR two readings 38.0 °C an hour apart with neutrophils under 0.5 x10^9/L) is a medical emergency requiring blood cultures and IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam within 60 minutes. Piperacillin-tazobactam is the AU first-line empirical choice; add vancomycin only for shock, line tunnel infection, severe mucositis, MRSA colonisation, or gram-positive growth. Meropenem is reserved for ESBL, recent broad-spectrum failure, or critical illness. Routine G-CSF is not indicated. ALL induction patients are admitted regardless of risk score.
key_points: Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy is AU first-line for stable paediatric febrile neutropenia
Antibiotic should be in within 60 minutes of arrival
Vancomycin add-on for shock, line, severe mucositis, MRSA, or gram-positive growth
Meropenem reserved for ESBL or critical illness
Induction-phase paediatric ALL patients always admitted for IV therapy
explanation.pearls: Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg per dose 6-hourly within 60 minutes of arrival is the AU paediatric febrile neutropenia first-line; door-to-antibiotic time is the auditable quality metric.

options.rationale: ChildKidsCAN and eviQ paediatric febrile neutropenia guidance recommends piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy as empirical first-line in haemodynamically stable children without focal severe infection or known resistant organism. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline; eviQ)

Ceftriaxone has no antipseudomonal activity and oral amoxicillin is inappropriate in a febrile neutropenic patient; AU paediatric guidance requires antipseudomonal IV cover empirically. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

Empirical vancomycin is reserved for shock, line infection, severe mucositis, MRSA-colonised patients, or gram-positive growth; routine empirical vancomycin is not indicated and aminoglycoside monotherapy is never appropriate. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

Meropenem is reserved for prior ESBL colonisation, recent broad-spectrum exposure, or critical illness; first-line stable febrile neutropenia is piperacillin-tazobactam. Routine G-CSF is not recommended empirically. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

Australian paediatric practice admits ALL children with febrile neutropenia for IV antibiotics; outpatient oral regimens for low-risk febrile neutropenia exist in adult/adolescent care but not as default in induction-phase paediatric ALL. (Source: ChildKidsCAN Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Hypercyanotic spells in tetralogy of Fallot arise from acute right ventricular outflow tract infundibular spasm with worsened right-to-left shunt across the VSD. The sequenced approach is knee-to-chest positioning (raises systemic vascular resistance), supplemental oxygen, and IV fluid bolus to increase preload. Morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm. Phenylephrine boluses (1-5 mcg/kg) raise systemic vascular resistance for refractory cases. Adrenaline is contraindicated because it worsens infundibular contraction; PGE1 has no role beyond the neonatal period.
key_points: Sequence: positioning, oxygen, IV fluids, morphine, then phenylephrine
Morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm
Adrenaline is contraindicated; phenylephrine raises SVR without infundibular spasm
PGE1 has no role after the ductus has closed in older infants
Refractory spells require intubation, paralysis, and urgent cardiology
explanation.pearls: In a hypercyanotic spell, the audible murmur quietens because right-to-left shunt has bypassed the RVOT; a previously loud murmur going silent is a marker of severity, not improvement.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.rationale: The ductus closes within days of birth and is not reopenable at 10 months of age; PGE1 has no role in hypercyanotic spells in an older infant with established tetralogy. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.rationale: Catecholamines increase infundibular contraction and worsen right ventricular outflow obstruction; adrenaline is contraindicated in unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot hypercyanotic spells. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.rationale: After knee-to-chest, oxygen, and IV fluids, morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV reduces hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm and is the recommended next step in unbroken hypercyanotic spells. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.rationale: Hypercyanotic spells reflect right-to-left shunt with reduced pulmonary blood flow, not pulmonary congestion; diuretics drop systemic vascular resistance and preload and worsen the spell. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for refractory acidosis after positioning, oxygen, fluid, morphine and phenylephrine have failed; it is not the next step ahead of morphine which addresses the mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease should be suspected in any neonate who has not passed meconium within 48 hours, or in an infant with chronic obstructive constipation, abdominal distension, and explosive release of stool after digital examination. Suction rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve trunks is the diagnostic gold standard. Contrast enema and anorectal manometry are supportive but not diagnostic. Definitive treatment is a pull-through procedure (Soave, Swenson, or Duhamel). Untreated Hirschsprung is complicated by enterocolitis, perforation, and death.
key_points: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours is a red flag for Hirschsprung disease
Explosive release of stool after PR is the classical clinical sign
Suction rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test
Contrast enema can suggest but not confirm the diagnosis
Hirschsprung enterocolitis is the leading cause of mortality before surgery
explanation.pearls: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours of life plus explosive release of stool after PR examination triggers suction rectal biopsy referral; the biopsy must be at least 2 cm above the dentate line to avoid the normal hypoganglionic zone.

options.rationale: Empirical laxative trial is appropriate for functional constipation but not for an infant with delayed meconium passage and explosive release on PR; functional constipation rarely begins in the first month of life. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours plus chronic obstructive constipation with explosive release on digital examination is Hirschsprung disease until proven otherwise; suction rectal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test. (Source: RACGP red book Paediatrics; RCH CPG: Constipation)

Meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis usually presents in the first 48 hours with bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium, not chronic explosive release on PR; this patient already has newborn screen and clinical features pointing to Hirschsprung. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Anorectal manometry is technically difficult in young infants and is a screening test in older children; AU practice goes directly to suction rectal biopsy for histology in infants with classical features. (Source: RACGP Paediatric Constipation Guidelines)

Contrast enema can suggest a transition zone but is not diagnostic and has poor sensitivity in neonates; histological confirmation by suction rectal biopsy is required before surgery is offered. (Source: RACGP Paediatric Constipation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Late-presenting urea cycle disorders (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is the most common) often manifest after a protein load or catabolic stress. The classical triad is encephalopathy, respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates the central respiratory drive), and absence of acidosis or hypoglycaemia. Plasma ammonia must be measured on a free-flowing sample placed on ice and run immediately. Above 400 micromol/L in a child with encephalopathy, extracorporeal removal (haemodialysis preferred, CRRT acceptable) is required alongside protein restriction, high-calorie dextrose, and intravenous ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate). Untreated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy carries a high risk of permanent neurological injury.
key_points: Respiratory alkalosis with encephalopathy in a child warrants an ammonia level
Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L plus encephalopathy is the threshold for dialysis
Scavengers reduce ammonia slowly; dialysis is the rapid intervention
Protein restriction and high-calorie dextrose stop endogenous protein catabolism
Family history of unexplained sibling death warrants high suspicion
explanation.pearls: Plasma ammonia must be measured on a free-flowing venous sample placed immediately on ice; falsely elevated levels are common with tourniquet use, haemolysis, or delayed laboratory transit.

options.rationale: Dextrose and lipid stop protein catabolism but do not remove ammonia from the circulation; ammonia at 480 micromol/L is acutely neurotoxic and requires extracorporeal removal alongside the metabolic measures. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol; RCH CPG: Metabolic Disorders)

Hyperammonaemia-induced cerebral oedema is treated by removing ammonia, not by osmotic therapy; mannitol does not address the underlying cause and delays definitive treatment. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

Scavengers are essential adjuncts but reduce ammonia too slowly when levels exceed 400 micromol/L; they are used alongside dialysis, not as a standalone strategy at this severity. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L with encephalopathy is the threshold for dialysis (haemodialysis preferred, CRRT acceptable); pharmacological scavengers alone cannot drop levels fast enough to avoid permanent neurological injury. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

Bacterial or viral encephalitis are reasonable differentials but the documented ammonia at 480 micromol/L and respiratory alkalosis pattern point to a urea cycle disorder; antibiotics alone do not treat the metabolic emergency. (Source: BIMDG Hyperammonaemia Protocol)

explanation.summary: Croup severity in Australia is stratified using the Westley framework: mild (no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession but calm), and severe (marked recession, agitation, or exhaustion). RCH gives a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for both mild and moderate croup. The higher 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe disease. Nebulised adrenaline is layered on top for severe croup and obligates a 3-hour observation window for rebound.
key_points: Stridor at rest plus calm child plus mild recession equals moderate croup
Mild and moderate croup share the same dexamethasone dose (0.15 mg/kg PO)
0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe disease and adds no benefit at lower severities
Nebulised adrenaline requires 3 hours of observation for rebound
explanation.pearls: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg acts within 30 minutes; a second dose is rarely indicated. Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe disease and mandate 3-hour observation after any nebulised adrenaline.

options.rationale: Stridor at rest with mild recession but no agitation places this child in the moderate Westley band. RCH directs a single oral dose of 0.15 mg/kg for both mild and moderate croup; onset is within 30 minutes and a second dose is rarely needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved by RCH for severe croup (stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, or hypoxia). Using it here would expose the child to four times the steroid load without added benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline is indicated for severe croup or impending obstruction, not moderate disease. Its benefit is short lived (30 to 90 minutes) and mandates 3-hour observation for rebound stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Beta-2 agonists target lower-airway smooth muscle and have no role in subglottic oedema. Reaching for salbutamol misclassifies stridor as wheeze. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
Even mild croup warrants a single dose of dexamethasone in current RCH guidance because it shortens illness and prevents return visits. Humidification has no evidence base. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: The RCH urinary tract infection guideline diverges from NICE on imaging after a first UTI. For a child over 6 months with a typical first UTI (E. coli, prompt response, no atypical features), no routine imaging is recommended provided antenatal scans were normal. Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical features. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade and are deployed only after recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound.
key_points: Typical first UTI in a child over 6 months requires no routine imaging at RCH
Atypical features that trigger acute ultrasound: non-E. coli, no response by 48 h, sepsis, abdominal mass, rising creatinine
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs not in the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI
Antenatal renal imaging history changes the threshold for any further imaging
explanation.pearls: RCH does not perform routine post-UTI ultrasound after the first typical infection over 6 months; reserve imaging for atypical features or recurrence within 6 months.

options.rationale: RCH reserves acute-phase ultrasound for atypical UTI features such as poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E. coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or rising creatinine. None of these apply. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

This is a typical first UTI in a child over 6 months with normal antenatal imaging and prompt response. RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, DMSA, or MCUG after a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

DMSA scanning sits in NICE pathways but is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI. Routine scarring screens add radiation without changing management here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, abnormal ultrasound findings, or atypical infection within the RCH cascade. It is not indicated after a single typical infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

Routine delayed ultrasound after a single typical UTI is a NICE construct that RCH does not adopt for children with normal antenatal imaging. It generates incidental findings with no management change. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary:
Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis and needs no investigations in a typical case. Fever, often to 38.5 degrees or higher, is part of the illness and does not on its own indicate bacterial co-infection, which is uncommon outside the first few weeks of life. Chest radiography is discouraged because atelectasis and peribronchial thickening are routinely misinterpreted as consolidation, which drives antibiotic prescribing without benefit. Management remains oxygen if required, feeding support and minimal handling, with reassessment if the trajectory changes.

In context: bronchiolitis is the commonest reason an Australian infant is admitted to hospital, and the PREDICT guideline was written largely to reduce interventions that do not help. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, antibiotics, chest radiography and routine blood tests are all outside standard care, and the discipline of not ordering them is itself the exam point.
key_points: Fever is expected in bronchiolitis and does not mandate antibiotics
Chest radiography is discouraged because it drives false positive readings
Bronchodilators, steroids and hypertonic saline are not recommended
Care is oxygen as needed, feeding support and minimal handling
explanation.pearls: The radiograph you order in typical bronchiolitis is the reason the antibiotic gets prescribed.

options.rationale: Fever is expected in bronchiolitis, and the PREDICT guideline advises against routine chest radiography or antibiotics because radiographic changes of bronchiolitis are readily misread as consolidation. (Source: PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline; RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

This is the regimen for a child with lobar pneumonia, meaning focal signs with high fever and toxicity, rather than the diffuse crackles and wheeze of a bronchiolitic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral amoxicillin is first-line for community-acquired pneumonia in a well enough child, which requires focal clinical or radiographic findings, not a viral bronchiolitic pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Empirical broad cover and cultures are for suspected serious bacterial infection, in practice an infant under 3 months with fever or any child who looks septic. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

A macrolide is reserved for suspected pertussis or atypical pneumonia, suggested by paroxysmal cough with whoop or apnoea in a young infant rather than by wheeze and crackles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) in children is usually self-limiting but renal involvement occurs in around 30 percent and drives long-term morbidity. Warning features that change management include hypertension above the 95th centile, nephrotic-range proteinuria (more than 2+ on dipstick or PCR >250 mg/mmol), and elevated creatinine. The presence of any of these triggers admission, blood-pressure control, and urgent paediatric nephrology referral with biopsy to grade nephritis and guide immunosuppression. Steroids treat abdominal and joint symptoms but do not prevent or treat nephritis.
key_points: HSP nephritis warning triad: hypertension, nephrotic-range proteinuria, raised creatinine
Most HSP is self-limiting; warning features change management entirely
Steroids do not prevent or treat nephritis - biopsy guides immunosuppression
Hypertension above the 95th centile for age and height needs immediate attention
explanation.pearls: HSP with proteinuria above 2+, hypertension above the 95th centile, or rising creatinine warrants paediatric nephrology referral within 24 hours for biopsy planning.

options.rationale: Although most HSP is self-limiting, this child shows three features that mandate escalation: hypertension above the 95th centile, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and an elevated creatinine. Routine community follow-up alone would miss progression to crescentic glomerulonephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Steroids may reduce abdominal pain in HSP but they do not prevent or treat established nephritis. Starting steroids before specialist assessment risks anchoring on the wrong therapy while serious renal disease evolves. (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines; RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

There is no infective source and the platelet count is normal, making sepsis or meningococcaemia unlikely. Empirical antibiotics here would not address the renal trajectory and add no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Hypertension, heavy proteinuria, and rising creatinine in HSP define warning features that prompt admission, blood-pressure control, and urgent nephrology referral for likely renal biopsy and immunosuppression planning. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura; KHA-CARI Guidelines)

Serology rarely reframes a textbook HSP presentation and there is no diagnostic uncertainty here that would justify deferring management for results. Time-to-biopsy is the live decision. (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Pre-transfer antibiotics for suspected meningococcal disease save lives. CDNA and Therapeutic Guidelines both endorse intramuscular benzylpenicillin (50 to 60 mg/kg to a maximum of 1.2 g) into the lateral thigh when IV access is delayed. Cultures and adjunctive corticosteroids do not gate the first dose. Intraosseous access remains the fastest reliable route for fluids and ongoing antibiotic infusions when IV attempts fail, but should not delay an IM dose if IO insertion itself is taking time.
key_points: IM benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg is endorsed when IV/IO access is delayed
Cultures and dexamethasone never gate the first antibiotic dose
RCH paediatric sepsis pathway: IV/IO access then cultures then antibiotic within the hour
Each hour of antibiotic delay measurably increases meningococcal mortality
explanation.pearls: When IV access is delayed in suspected meningococcal sepsis, give IM benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg (max 1.2 g) into the lateral thigh while IO insertion proceeds in parallel.

options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics for cultures in suspected meningococcal disease worsens mortality. Cultures are taken at the same time as IO access but never gate the first antibiotic dose. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline)

Adjunctive dexamethasone in paediatric meningitis is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, not as a standalone first move, and the antibiotic remains the time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

When IV access is delayed in suspected meningococcal sepsis, the CDNA guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines explicitly endorse intramuscular benzylpenicillin immediately while access is being secured. Pre-transfer antibiotics reduce mortality. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Each hour of antibiotic delay in invasive meningococcal disease increases mortality. CDNA mandates antibiotic administration at the point of suspicion, never withheld for retrieval. (Source: CDNA Invasive Meningococcal Disease Guideline)

Repeated peripheral attempts after two failures waste time. The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway calls for intraosseous access after failed IV and intramuscular antibiotics if even IO is delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA with circulatory compromise sits in a deliberately separate fluid-resuscitation pathway. RCH and ISPAD specify 10 mL/kg boluses of 0.9 percent saline over 30 to 60 minutes, with reassessment after each bolus, instead of the 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 minutes used in septic shock. The reason is cerebral oedema, the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality, which is precipitated by rapid osmotic shifts. Insulin is delayed at least 1 hour after fluid commencement and bicarbonate is contraindicated.
key_points: DKA shock bolus: 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes (NOT 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 min)
Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of paediatric DKA mortality
Insulin starts at least 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins
Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA with shock, give 10 mL/kg of saline over 30 to 60 minutes (not the standard 20 mL/kg over 5 to 10 minutes used in septic shock) to limit cerebral-oedema risk.

options.rationale: Insulin in DKA must follow at least one fluid bolus, and is typically delayed 1 to 2 hours after fluid restoration begins. Starting insulin before fluid resuscitation precipitates cardiovascular collapse and worsens cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

Standard septic-shock bolus volumes in DKA are linked to cerebral oedema and worsened neurological outcomes. RCH and ISPAD explicitly halve the bolus in this context. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022)

Hartmann's solution is acceptable as maintenance fluid in DKA but the bolus rate is the live problem here. A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus carries the same cerebral-oedema risk regardless of crystalloid choice. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022)

RCH and ISPAD specify cautious 10 mL/kg boluses over 30 to 60 minutes in DKA with circulatory compromise, to limit the cerebral-oedema risk that rapid fluid shifts trigger. Reassess after each bolus rather than running standard sepsis volumes. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis; ISPAD 2022)

Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA because it worsens cerebral oedema, paradoxical CNS acidosis, and hypokalaemia. It is not part of any current RCH or ISPAD pathway. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022)

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia (GALT deficiency) presents in the first two weeks of life with E. coli sepsis (a near-pathognomonic association), conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, and bilateral cataracts. Urinary reducing substances are positive while the glucose oxidase strip is negative. Treatment is dual: aggressive treatment of sepsis with standard neonatal cover (IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin) AND immediate removal of dietary galactose by switching to a soy-based formula while definitive GALT enzyme assay is processed. Delay in either limb causes irreversible injury.
key_points: Galactosaemia neonate presents with E. coli sepsis, jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, cataracts
Urine reducing substances positive while glucose oxidase strip negative is the bedside clue
Treat sepsis AND remove dietary galactose simultaneously - both are time-critical
Soy-based formula is the Australian standard substitute
explanation.pearls: Suspect classical galactosaemia in any neonate with E. coli sepsis plus jaundice plus hypoglycaemia plus positive urinary reducing substances; switch immediately to soy-based formula while awaiting GALT enzyme assay.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.rationale: Although the antibiotic regimen is correct for neonatal sepsis, continuing lactose-containing feeds will perpetuate galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, deepen the encephalopathy, and worsen the liver injury. The feeds must change at the same time. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

Hydrolysed cow's milk formula still contains lactose and does not solve the galactose problem. Amoxicillin alone does not cover all relevant Gram-negative sepsis pathogens; benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

Newborn screening reports may take days to weeks; in classical galactosaemia, ongoing galactose exposure causes irreversible cataracts, liver failure, and brain injury during that window. Empirical feed change is mandatory once the diagnosis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

Phototherapy addresses unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not the conjugated picture seen here, and does not address galactose exposure. Awaiting GALT enzyme assay before changing feeds delays the only modifiable cause of ongoing injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders)

Suspected classical galactosaemia (E. coli sepsis, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hypoglycaemia, cataracts, positive urinary reducing substances) demands immediate removal of lactose and galactose while sepsis is treated and metabolic confirmation is sought. (Source: RCH CPG: Inherited metabolic disorders; Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: ASCIA anaphylaxis dosing uses a banded age and weight table rather than per kg arithmetic to reduce dosing errors during resuscitation. The 7.5 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms IM (the EpiPen Jr dose); the 20 kg and above band receives 300 micrograms IM (the standard EpiPen dose). All children with airway, breathing, or circulatory features get IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh as the first action, before fluids or steroids. Repeat at 5 minutes if no improvement; consider IV infusion after two failed IM doses.
key_points: ASCIA uses a banded IM dose table: 7.5 to 20 kg gets 150 micrograms, 20 kg and above gets 300 micrograms
Anterolateral thigh IM is faster and more reliable than subcutaneous or deltoid injection
IV adrenaline is third-line and only after two failed IM doses, as a diluted infusion with monitoring
Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway obstruction, not systemic anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: ASCIA IM adrenaline by band: 7.5 to 20 kg gets 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr); 20 kg and above gets 300 micrograms (EpiPen). Repeat IM at 5 minutes if no improvement before escalating to an IV infusion.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: An 18 kg child falls within the ASCIA 7.5 to 20 kg band, which prescribes 150 micrograms IM (EpiPen Jr equivalent) into the mid anterolateral thigh. The banded table is the AU standard and avoids the dosing errors that occur with weight-based calculation in a stressed resus. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: 300 micrograms is the ASCIA dose for the 20 kg and above band. At 18 kg this is twice the indicated dose and risks tachyarrhythmia and hypertension. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses have failed and must be given as a diluted infusion with cardiac monitoring. First-line is always IM into the anterolateral thigh. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable than IM in shock. ASCIA explicitly recommends IM (not subcut) in the anterolateral thigh. Weight-based 10 microgram per kg arithmetic is also not the ASCIA standard. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema in croup, not systemic anaphylaxis. It does not address hypotension, shock, or peripheral vasodilation and delays definitive IM dosing. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway runs as a sequenced first-hour bundle: recognise sepsis, secure IV/IO access, draw blood cultures, give the first IV antibiotic within the hour, and start 20 mL/kg saline boluses over 5 to 10 minutes up to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes follow fluid-refractory shock. The order matters because each step has an independent mortality signal and antibiotics should not be held for cultures if access is difficult.
key_points: Order: IV access, cultures, antibiotics, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Up to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid before declaring fluid-refractory shock and starting inotropes
10 mL/kg is the DKA and neonatal-cardiac starting bolus, not the septic shock bolus
Antibiotics within the first hour of recognition; do not delay for cultures if access is hard
explanation.pearls: RCH paediatric sepsis: 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes (up to 60 mL/kg total), first IV antibiotic within the hour, inotropes only after fluid-refractory shock. Do not delay antibiotics for cultures if access is difficult.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences IV/IO access first, then blood cultures, then the first antibiotic dose within the hour, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes (repeat to 60 mL/kg). Cultures are taken before antibiotics only if it does not delay them. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Although fluids and antibiotics both belong in the first hour, RCH places the first antibiotic dose immediately after cultures and before the fluid bolus where access permits. Delaying antibiotics for a bolus worsens mortality in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock (no improvement after 40 to 60 mL/kg). Starting adrenaline before any fluid is given inverts the RCH and ANZICS paediatric sepsis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: Stress-dose steroids are considered only in catecholamine-refractory shock or known adrenal insufficiency. Empiric steroids are not first-line and delay the source-directed antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.rationale: A 10 mL/kg bolus is the RCH starting volume for DKA and for neonates with suspected cardiac disease, not for paediatric septic shock. Antibiotics must not wait for the bolus to complete. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

explanation.summary:
In a child with gastroenteritis and no more than minimal dehydration, feeding advice is simple and is one of the few interventions that changes the course of the illness. Breastfeeding continues unchanged, formula is given at usual strength without dilution, and an age-appropriate solid diet is resumed early rather than after a starvation period. Extra fluid is offered to replace ongoing losses, using oral rehydration solution rather than juice or soft drink because of their sugar load and low sodium content.

In context: acute gastroenteritis in Australian children is predominantly viral, with rotavirus much reduced since the introduction of routine immunisation and norovirus now prominent. Management is entirely supportive: maintain hydration, keep feeding, avoid antimotility agents and antibiotics, and give parents clear advice about the signs of dehydration that should bring the child back.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding and give formula at normal strength
Resume an age-appropriate diet early rather than withholding food
Use oral rehydration solution for extra losses, not juice or soft drink
Antimotility agents are not used in children
explanation.pearls: The old advice to rest the gut costs weight and prolongs the diarrhoea; feeding through the illness is the treatment, not a concession to it.

options.rationale: RCH and Therapeutic Guidelines both advise continuing breastfeeding through gastroenteritis and resuming an age-appropriate diet early, which shortens illness and preserves the mucosa. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

A clear fluid only period is sometimes needed for a few hours in a child vomiting everything, but breast milk is never withheld; it is well tolerated and provides both fluid and energy. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Prolonged food withholding was historical practice and is now avoided; a period without solids is reasonable only while a child is actively vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
