A lactose free formula is considered for a formula fed infant with prolonged watery diarrhoea and perianal excoriation after the acute illness, not routinely at presentation and not for a breastfed infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Juice is hyperosmolar and low in sodium, so it worsens osmotic diarrhoea. Diluted juice has a limited role only where rehydration solution is refused and dehydration is minimal. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 3 months are at substantially higher risk of invasive bacterial infection and meningitis than older children. RCH mandates a full septic workup (blood culture, urine catheter specimen, FBC, CRP, and lumbar puncture) for any febrile infant under 4 weeks and for unwell-appearing infants between 1 and 3 months. Empiric IV cefotaxime (or per local pathway) is started after specimens are taken. Recent immunisation is NOT a reason to defer the workup at this age.
key_points: Under 4 weeks: full septic workup including LP regardless of appearance
1 to 3 months: full workup if unwell appearing or raised inflammatory markers
Post-immunisation fever does not exclude sepsis in this age group
Empiric cefotaxime after specimens; ampicillin added if under 4 weeks for Listeria cover
explanation.pearls: Under 3 months febrile: full septic workup including LP if unwell or raised CRP. Empiric IV cefotaxime; add ampicillin if under 4 weeks. Post-immunisation timing does not exempt from workup.

options.rationale: Procalcitonin can refine risk in 1 to 3 month infants alongside other parameters but cannot exclude meningitis in an unwell appearing 5-week-old. RCH does not endorse single-marker rule out at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

Post-immunisation fever can occur but RCH explicitly does NOT use the timing as an exclusion criterion for sepsis workup in an infant under 3 months. Clinical features here (high-pitched cry, reduced feeds, raised CRP) demand the full workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)
A catheter urine specimen is part of the full septic screen but is not sufficient alone. RCH requires blood cultures and an LP added on top in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

RCH directs a full septic workup including lumbar puncture for any febrile infant under 4 weeks, and strongly recommends it under 3 months when the infant is unwell, has a high-pitched cry, or has a CRP raised above local thresholds. Recent immunisation does not exclude bacterial sepsis at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)
Cranial ultrasound is used for haemorrhage and hydrocephalus screening, not for diagnosing CNS infection. CSF analysis remains the diagnostic test. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception classically presents in 3 to 36-month-olds with paroxysmal inconsolable crying with leg drawing, pallor, and later redcurrant-jelly stool. Ultrasound shows a target or doughnut lesion and is diagnostic. Treatment of stable cases is pneumatic (air) enema reduction by an experienced paediatric radiologist with surgical backup. Indications for surgery are failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation, or a pathological lead point.
key_points: Ultrasound target lesion is diagnostic in 3 to 36-month-olds with intermittent distress
Pneumatic (air) enema is preferred over hydrostatic; barium is obsolete
Surgery for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point
IV access and fluid status should be optimised before enema reduction
explanation.pearls: Stable ileocolic intussusception: pneumatic enema reduction under fluoroscopy by a paediatric radiologist. Surgery only for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or pathological lead point.

options.rationale: Untreated intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia, perforation, and shock. Conservative observation is not a valid strategy once the diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Surgery is the next step only after failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation, or a pathological lead point on imaging. Going directly to laparotomy in a stable child with a successfully imaged target lesion exposes the child to an unnecessary operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Stable ileocolic intussusception without peritonism or perforation is treated by air (pneumatic) enema reduction. RCH and the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons paediatric guidance prefer pneumatic over hydrostatic in most centres given higher reduction rates and lower contamination risk. Surgery is reserved for failed enema, peritonism, or perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
The target lesion on ultrasound is already diagnostic. Delay introduces ischaemia risk and is not RCH practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Barium has been replaced by air or water-soluble contrast because of peritoneal contamination risk if perforation occurs. The diagnosis is already established; the question is reduction modality. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Acute ITP in a well child after a viral prodrome with isolated thrombocytopenia, a clean film, no lymphadenopathy, and no organomegaly is managed by observation alone irrespective of the count if bleeding is cutaneous or minor mucosal. Most resolve within 6 weeks. IVIG, anti-D, or steroids are reserved for active mucosal, gastrointestinal, intracranial, or other significant bleeding, or to raise the count rapidly before a procedure. Platelet transfusions are ineffective due to antibody-mediated clearance and reserved for life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: Watchful waiting is HSANZ first-line in well children with cutaneous bleeding only
Treatment is driven by bleeding severity, not by the absolute platelet count
IVIG, anti-D, or corticosteroids for active mucosal or major bleeding
Routine marrow examination is not required in classic acute ITP with a clean film
explanation.pearls: Paediatric ITP: cutaneous-only bleeding is observed; IVIG 0.8 g/kg or prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for active mucosal bleeding. Platelet transfusions are reserved for life-threatening bleeding only.

options.rationale: Routine marrow examination is not required in classic acute ITP with a clean film and isolated thrombocytopenia. It is reserved for atypical features, treatment failure, or before steroids in some centres. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

IVIG is reserved by HSANZ for active mucosal or visceral bleeding or for raising the count quickly before a procedure. Skin and minor palatal petechiae alone do not justify it. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

Corticosteroids work in ITP but masking a missed leukaemia would delay diagnosis if the film were not first carefully reviewed. With a clean film, steroids may still be used for mucosal bleeding; cutaneous-only disease does not need them. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

First-episode acute ITP in a well child with cutaneous bleeding only is managed with observation under the HSANZ and Australian and New Zealand Childhood Haematology Oncology Group consensus. Most resolve within weeks. Treatment is reserved for active mucosal or major bleeding, not for the platelet count alone. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

Platelet transfusions are ineffective in ITP because the antibody clears infused platelets and are reserved for life-threatening bleeding only. They are not a count-raising intervention here. (Source: HSANZ Paediatric ITP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Initial oxygen support in moderate bronchiolitis is low-flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 90 percent or above, with high-flow reserved for failure of low-flow after a trial period. Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids do not change outcomes in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months. High-flow is not the starting point in moderate bronchiolitis.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is at or above 90 percent, not 92 to 94 percent.
Low-flow oxygen first, HFNC after 1 to 2 hours of failed low-flow.
No role for salbutamol or ipratropium under 12 months in bronchiolitis.
Steroids and hypertonic saline are not recommended.
explanation.pearls: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 at or above 90 percent is first-line in bronchiolitis under RCH CPG; reassess at 1 to 2 hours before escalating to HFNC.

sources.label: Cochrane review of bronchodilators in bronchiolitis

options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance directs low-flow nasal prong oxygen (typically 1 to 2 L/min) as the first respiratory support with an SpO2 target of 90 percent or above. High-flow is reserved for failure of low-flow after a defined trial. Starting low-flow first prevents premature escalation and the associated nursing acuity. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for infants who fail low-flow oxygen after 1 to 2 hours of trial or who are showing severe respiratory distress. The SpO2 target in RCH guidance is 90 percent and above, not 92 to 94 percent, so starting at HFNC with a tighter target overshoots the cascade. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

Inhaled bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because the wheeze is from airway oedema and debris, not bronchospasm. Trials show no clinically meaningful improvement and risk of tachycardia masking deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

Nebulised hypertonic saline is not recommended in RCH guidance for routine bronchiolitis management; the limited evidence does not support meaningful reduction in admission length, and it can trigger bronchospasm. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

Corticosteroids are not indicated in bronchiolitis. Cochrane and RCH guidance both find no benefit on admission rate or length of stay, and there is concern about prolonged viral shedding. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Severe acute asthma not responding to continuous bronchodilator, ipratropium, and systemic steroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes. IV salbutamol and aminophylline are subsequent rungs of the ladder. Intubation is reserved for impending arrest features which are absent here.
key_points: IV magnesium dose in paediatric severe asthma: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes.
Order: continuous salbutamol + ipratropium + oral steroid -> IV magnesium -> IV salbutamol -> IV aminophylline.
Silent chest, exhaustion, falling GCS = impending arrest, intubate.
IM adrenaline only if no IV access or impending arrest.
explanation.pearls: When inhaled therapy plus oral prednisolone fails in paediatric severe asthma, the next step is IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring; IV salbutamol and aminophylline follow.

options.rationale: Aminophylline is reserved for asthma not responding to magnesium and salbutamol infusion. It has a narrow therapeutic window and significant cardiac and CNS toxicity, so it sits later in the cascade. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

IV salbutamol is an option after IV magnesium has been trialled or when magnesium is unavailable or contraindicated. It carries higher risks of hypokalaemia and arrhythmia, so the cascade recommends magnesium first. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

After failure of maximal inhaled therapy and systemic corticosteroid in severe acute asthma, IV magnesium sulfate is the next-line bronchodilator in the AU paediatric pathway. Dose is 50 mg/kg up to 2 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring. Evidence supports reduction in admission and need for ventilation. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

IM adrenaline is reserved for severe asthma with impending respiratory arrest or where IV access is not yet established. The child has IV access already and is not in arrest. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory arrest (silent chest, exhaustion, falling GCS, marked acidosis). The child is alert, cooperative, and improving on inhaled therapy. Premature intubation in severe asthma worsens outcomes. (Source: RCH CPG Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: In a child older than 6 months with a single typical E coli UTI that responded to oral antibiotics and a documented normal antenatal renal ultrasound, RCH guidance does not require renal tract imaging or prophylactic antibiotics. Imaging is reserved for atypical features, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. Atypical features include poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E coli organisms, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine. DMSA and MCUG sit outside the RCH cascade and are not pursued in this scenario.
key_points: RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI over 6 months of age.
Atypical UTI = poor response to 48 h antibiotics, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine.
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade.
Antibiotic prophylaxis after a single UTI is not indicated.
explanation.pearls: After a first typical paediatric UTI in a child over 6 months with antenatal monitoring documented, no renal tract imaging and no antibiotic prophylaxis are required under RCH CPG.

options.rationale: MCUG is invasive, involves bladder catheterisation and significant radiation, and is not recommended after a single typical UTI in RCH guidance. It is also outside the RCH cascade as DMSA is. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

Routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI is not in the RCH cascade for children over 6 months who had a clinical response and a normal antenatal scan. Imaging here would only be indicated if features of atypical UTI (poor response to 48 hours of antibiotics, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine) were present. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH UTI imaging cascade for paediatric AU practice. They are derived from NICE pathways; following RCH consistently is preferred over mixing AU and UK protocols. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

RCH guidance does not recommend renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a child over 6 months who responded promptly to antibiotics and had antenatal monitoring. Imaging is reserved for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first typical UTI in a child over 6 months. The PRIVENT trial and RCH guidance found no meaningful benefit, with antimicrobial resistance risk; reserve for selected children with recurrent UTI and reflux. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

explanation.summary: Witnessed choking with persistent unilateral respiratory signs and air trapping on expiratory chest x-ray is a clinical diagnosis of inhaled foreign body. Cashews are radiolucent, so plain films cannot rule it out. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: Inspiratory and expiratory films show air trapping on the affected side in ball-valve obstruction.
Cashews and peanuts are radiolucent; absence of opacity does not exclude airway foreign body.
Back blows and chest thrusts are first-aid for active choking, not stable children with localised signs.
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the standard of care.
explanation.pearls: Persistent unilateral wheeze and chest x-ray air trapping after witnessed choking go straight to rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia; do not delay for CT or trial bronchodilators.

options.rationale: Treating localised wheeze with bronchodilators when foreign body is the leading diagnosis delays definitive care and risks the object moving into a more compromising location. Salbutamol does not displace an inhaled foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

CT can be confirmatory in equivocal cases but adds delay and radiation when the history and inspiratory or expiratory films are already diagnostic. The next intervention is therapeutic (rigid bronchoscopy), not further imaging. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

The combination of witnessed choking, persistent unilateral signs, and x-ray demonstrating ball-valve obstruction is diagnostic of an airway foreign body until proven otherwise. Definitive diagnosis and removal both occur at rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Cashews are radiolucent so plain films cannot exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

Back blows and chest thrusts are first-aid for an actively choking child with a partially or completely obstructed airway. The child is now stable with localised signs, so blind manoeuvres can move the object centrally and create complete obstruction. (Source: ANZCOR Paediatric BLS guideline)

Observation without removal delays definitive diagnosis and increases the risk of distal migration, complete obstruction, or pneumonitis from oils in the nut. Rigid bronchoscopy is the standard of care once foreign body is the leading diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG Foreign body airway)

explanation.summary: Failed image-guided reduction of intussusception (typically after two attempts or in the face of partial reduction) is an indication for operative reduction. The surgical team performs manual reduction in theatre and resects non-viable bowel. Delaying further or trying additional non-operative attempts raises perforation risk.
key_points: Two failed enema attempts (or persistent partial reduction) is a surgical indication.
Perforation risk rises with repeated enema attempts.
Operative approach is laparotomy or laparoscopy with manual reduction.
Cover with antibiotics is adjunct, not a temporising substitute.
explanation.pearls: After two failed pneumatic reduction attempts or persistent partial reduction in intussusception, take the child to theatre for laparotomy and manual reduction; further enema attempts increase perforation risk.

options.rationale: Antibiotics are appropriate as adjunct cover once a decision for surgery is made, but they are not a substitute for operative reduction. Waiting 12 hours for re-imaging risks bowel ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

RCH guidance limits enema attempts to two or three depending on local protocol, but continued attempts in the face of partial reduction increase perforation risk and delay definitive care. With failure documented and partial reduction only, theatre is now the standard. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

Switching modality (hydrostatic versus pneumatic) is not generally salvage after a documented partial reduction failure; centres pick one approach per local resources. Persisting with imaging-guided reduction now adds delay. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

Conservative observation after a failed reduction is not appropriate because the bowel remains at risk of ischaemia and perforation. The intervention has not resolved the invagination. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

After two failed attempts at pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction in a haemodynamically stable child without perforation, the next step is operative reduction. The surgeon will perform manual reduction and resect non-viable bowel if necessary. Continuing to attempt reduction beyond two failed cycles increases the risk of perforation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid in the vomitus. The alkalosis is a contraindication to general anaesthesia because of post-operative apnoea risk, so the infant is resuscitated to biochemical safety before pyloromyotomy. Targets are bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L. Resuscitation fluid is 0.9 percent saline with potassium replacement once urine output is established.
key_points: Pre-operative biochemistry targets: bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L.
Initial fluid is 0.9 percent saline with potassium replacement once urine output established.
Alkalosis predisposes to central respiratory depression after anaesthesia.
Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency.
explanation.pearls: Correct the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis of pyloric stenosis with 0.9 percent saline and potassium replacement before pyloromyotomy; aim for bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L.

options.rationale: Oral intake in a child with gastric outlet obstruction is ineffective for resuscitation because the fluid will not pass the pylorus. Intravenous resuscitation is required. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

Operating on an alkalotic infant predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea. The dehydration is not an obstructed abdomen with bowel ischaemia; there is time to resuscitate. RCH guidance is clear that biochemical correction precedes operation. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)
NGT decompression is reasonable adjunct but does not address the metabolic alkalosis. Time-pressured operation in an alkalotic infant raises post-op apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

Pyloric stenosis is a medical resuscitation that becomes a surgical case, not the reverse. The hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic, metabolic alkalosis must be corrected before general anaesthesia because alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea through central respiratory depression. The accepted biochemical thresholds for theatre are bicarbonate below 30 and chloride above 100 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

Acid suppression does not address the urgent biochemical derangement that drives the post-anaesthetic apnoea risk. It is also not part of the standard pre-operative pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with palpable faecal mass requires oral disimpaction with macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at an escalating dose for 3 to 7 days, followed by daily maintenance for at least 6 months. Failure to disimpact before maintenance is the most common reason for treatment failure. Dietary advice and a low-dose osmotic alone are inadequate when impaction is already established. Red flags for organic disease prompt further investigation but are absent in this child.
key_points: Disimpaction: macrogol 3350 with electrolytes, escalating regimen over 3 to 7 days.
Maintenance: macrogol 3350 daily for at least 6 months, weaned gradually.
Red flags for organic disease: failure to thrive, delayed meconium, bilious vomiting, abnormal neurology, sacral dimple or hair tuft.
Abdominal x-ray is not required when the abdomen is examinable.
explanation.pearls: Use macrogol 3350 with electrolytes for both disimpaction (escalating dose over 3 to 7 days) and maintenance (daily dose for 6 months); enemas and dietary advice alone fail because the withheld stool reservoir is not cleared.

options.rationale: Dietary advice and a low-dose osmotic alone are inadequate where there is established faecal impaction. The withheld stool reservoir must be cleared before maintenance becomes effective. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

Functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction before maintenance. RCH recommends macrogol 3350 with electrolytes (Movicol Junior or equivalent) at an escalating dose over 3 to 7 days, then a daily maintenance dose for at least 6 months. Maintenance therapy alone without disimpaction repeatedly fails. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

Phosphate enemas are associated with electrolyte derangement and trauma in children and are not first-line for disimpaction in the AU paediatric pathway. Oral macrogol disimpaction is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

Stimulant laxatives alone are not first-line for disimpaction. They are useful as adjuncts to osmotics in selected maintenance regimens but do not clear faecal mass effectively. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

Faecal impaction is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by abdominal examination and history. Abdominal x-ray is not routinely required and adds radiation without changing management. The presentation lacks red flags for organic disease that would justify subspecialist referral. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis develops up to 6 months after initial presentation and can be silent in its early stages. RCH recommends weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months, with escalation if proteinuria, hypertension or worsening renal function emerges. Biopsy is reserved for significant proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine.
key_points: Renal surveillance after HSP runs for 6 months from onset.
Weekly urinalysis and BP for first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months.
Quantify proteinuria with ACR or PCR if dipstick positive.
Biopsy indications: nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, declining renal function.
explanation.pearls: Schedule weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 1 to 2 months then monthly to 6 months in HSP; nephritis can be silent and biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria or progressive disease.

options.rationale: Renal imaging is reserved for established nephritis or in atypical clinical course. The primary screen is dipstick urinalysis with quantitative urine ACR or PCR if positive, plus blood pressure. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

HSP nephritis can be silent in its early stages with microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria as the only signs. Waiting for symptomatic disease misses the treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

RCH guidance recommends close renal surveillance after HSP because nephritis can develop late (up to 6 months after onset). Urinalysis and blood pressure weekly for the first 1 to 2 months, then monthly to 6 months, picks up evolving nephritis at the point where treatment intensification is meaningful. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
Daily urinalysis is impractical and not supported by evidence. Weekly testing in the first months catches evolving disease without burdening the family. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

Renal biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, or progressive renal dysfunction. A child with HSP and no renal findings does not need a biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when there is fever for 5 or more days with 2 or 3 classical features plus supportive laboratory findings (raised CRP and ESR, anaemia, thrombocytosis, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria) or a coronary artery z-score of 2.5 or above. First-line treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin. Treatment should not be delayed beyond day 10 if there is ongoing inflammation or evolving coronary involvement. Corticosteroids and infliximab are adjuncts or rescue therapy rather than substitutes for IVIG.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever 5 or more days + 2 to 3 classical features + supportive labs OR coronary z-score 2.5 or above.
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is first-line, even after day 10 if active inflammation persists.
Steroids are adjunct in high-risk patients (Kobayashi score positive) but not a substitute for IVIG.
Infliximab is for IVIG-resistant disease.
explanation.pearls: Incomplete Kawasaki with coronary z-score 2.5 or above mandates IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin even past day 10; steroids and biologics are adjuncts or rescue, not substitutes.

options.rationale: Observation is not appropriate when the criteria for incomplete Kawasaki are met and coronary changes are present. Delay risks progression to coronary aneurysm. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

This is incomplete Kawasaki disease - fever 5 or more days with 2 or 3 classical features, supportive laboratory findings, and now coronary artery z-score 2.5 or above on echocardiogram. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be commenced once the diagnosis is established, even after day 10 if there is ongoing inflammation or coronary involvement. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement; RCH CPG Kawasaki)

Corticosteroids are an adjunct to or rescue therapy after IVIG, not a substitute for first-line treatment in non-high-risk patients. They are also used as primary adjunct in high-risk patients (Kobayashi score positive) but in addition to, not instead of, IVIG. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)
Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki after a first or second dose of IVIG has failed. It is not first-line therapy. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

Broad antibiotics have been trialled empirically with no response and cultures are negative. Withholding IVIG to chase an occult bacterial source is not justified when criteria for incomplete Kawasaki are met. (Source: AHA Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

explanation.summary: Newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with cutaneous bleeding alone is managed with observation, bleeding precautions, and serial platelet counts irrespective of the absolute platelet number. Active treatment (IVIG, steroids, anti-D) is reserved for mucosal or organ bleeding or for procedures. Bone marrow biopsy is not routine when the clinical and laboratory picture is typical.
key_points: Treatment decisions in ITP are guided by bleeding phenotype, not platelet count.
Cutaneous-only bleeding is managed with observation even if platelets are below 20 x10^9/L.
IVIG, steroids, and anti-D are reserved for mucosal or organ bleeding.
Most paediatric ITP resolves within 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Manage cutaneous-only newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with watch and wait plus bleeding precautions; treat only for wet purpura, mucosal bleeding, or procedure preparation per ASH paediatric ITP guidance.

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in ITP is reserved for life-threatening bleeding because transfused platelets are also rapidly destroyed by the autoantibody. It does not address the underlying immune mechanism. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

IVIG raises platelets faster but does not improve clinical outcomes in cutaneous-only ITP. It is reserved for active mucosal or organ bleeding and for procedures requiring haemostasis. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

Corticosteroids raise platelet count but have steroid side effects and do not change long-term outcomes in cutaneous-only disease. Reserve for active bleeding or imminent procedures. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

Newly diagnosed paediatric ITP with cutaneous bleeding only (no wet purpura, no mucosal or major bleeding) is managed with observation regardless of platelet count. Bleeding outcomes correlate with bleeding phenotype, not the platelet number. Most cases resolve within 6 months. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines; RCH CPG ITP)

Bone marrow biopsy is not required when the clinical picture and blood film are typical of ITP. Reserve for atypical features such as lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, abnormal red or white cell line, or failure to respond to treatment. (Source: ASH ITP guidelines)

explanation.summary: New-onset Type 1 diabetes without DKA is treated with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting with meals), inpatient admission for multidisciplinary diabetes education, and structured outpatient follow-up. IV insulin and large fluid resuscitation belong to the DKA pathway. Treating this non-acidotic, clinically stable child as DKA overtreats and adds risk of hypoglycaemia. Basal-bolus is preferred over twice-daily premixed insulin from diagnosis under ISPAD guidance.
key_points: DKA requires venous pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L plus ketosis.
Without DKA: subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration, education.
Basal-bolus is preferred over twice-daily premix from diagnosis.
Metformin has no role in established Type 1 diabetes.
explanation.pearls: New paediatric Type 1 diabetes without DKA gets subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and inpatient education; IV insulin is the DKA pathway and is unnecessary here.

options.rationale: Newly diagnosed paediatric T1DM is admitted for inpatient initiation, diabetes education, parental skill development (injection technique, carbohydrate counting, hypoglycaemia management), and arrangement of community follow-up. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

An IV insulin infusion is the DKA pathway. This child does not meet DKA criteria (pH 7.36, bicarbonate 23, ketones 0.5). Treating him as DKA is overtreatment that risks hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

Twice-daily premixed insulin is less physiological and produces inferior glycaemic outcomes compared with basal-bolus in newly diagnosed paediatric T1DM. AU and ISPAD guidance favour basal-bolus or pump therapy from diagnosis. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

Metformin is not first-line for Type 1 diabetes; insulin is mandatory because of absolute insulin deficiency. The diagnosis is clinically Type 1 based on age, weight loss, and ketosis. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

Newly diagnosed Type 1 diabetes without DKA is treated with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (long-acting basal plus rapid-acting with meals) and diabetes education from the multidisciplinary team. IV insulin is reserved for DKA. The child is alert, eating, and not acidotic. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines)

explanation.summary: A salt-losing adrenal crisis in undiagnosed classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) presents with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock around 1 to 2 weeks of age. Treatment is immediate IV hydrocortisone (stress dose) and isotonic dextrose-saline resuscitation. Diagnostic samples are sent in parallel, not as a prerequisite to treatment.
key_points: Hydrocortisone stress dose under 1 year: 25 mg IV bolus then 25 mg every 6 hours.
Dexamethasone is avoided as it suppresses 17-OHP and lacks mineralocorticoid effect.
Fludrocortisone is oral only; intravenous mineralocorticoid replacement is not available.
Send 17-OHP, electrolytes, glucose, karyotype in parallel with treatment, not before.
explanation.pearls: Treat suspected paediatric salt-losing CAH crisis with IV hydrocortisone (25 mg for infants under 1 year) plus 0.9 percent saline with 10 percent dextrose bolus; never delay for confirmatory bloods, and avoid dexamethasone because it suppresses 17-OHP.

options.rationale: This is a salt-losing adrenal crisis in classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency). Hydrocortisone (stress dose 25 mg IV for infants under 1 year per AU paediatric endocrine guidance) is given immediately, followed by isotonic saline with dextrose to address hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is added once oral intake is established. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines; RCH CPG Adrenal crisis)

Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and would not address the salt-wasting component of this crisis. Hydrocortisone, which has both glucocorticoid and weak mineralocorticoid activity, is the standard. Dexamethasone is also avoided in suspected CAH because it suppresses the 17-OHP result. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

Calcium gluconate is reserved for hyperkalaemic ECG changes; potassium 6.8 mmol/L without ECG features in CAH crisis is treated upstream by hydrocortisone and saline correction. Treating only the potassium misses the underlying steroid deficit and risks deterioration. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

Fludrocortisone is not available as an intravenous preparation in Australia. Mineralocorticoid replacement is given orally once the infant is feeding; the acute crisis is managed with IV hydrocortisone, which has weak mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

Investigations are sent in parallel with treatment, not before it. Withholding stress hydrocortisone in a haemodynamically compromised infant with biochemistry typical of adrenal crisis is unsafe; treat first, confirm later. (Source: APEG congenital adrenal hyperplasia guidelines)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the most serious complication of paediatric DKA, presenting with headache, altered consciousness, and the Cushing response (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration). Treatment is immediate: reduce IV fluid rate by one-third and give 3 percent hypertonic saline (2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes) or mannitol (0.5 to 1 g/kg). Treatment must not wait for imaging.
key_points: Triad of bradycardia, hypertension, and altered consciousness in DKA = cerebral oedema.
First step: reduce fluid rate by one-third and give hyperosmolar therapy.
Hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 3 percent solution OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg.
Imaging follows stabilisation, not before.
explanation.pearls: DKA cerebral oedema is signalled by headache plus Cushing response and is treated immediately with one-third reduction in IV fluids plus 3 percent hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes per ISPAD; do not delay for CT.

options.rationale: Adding dextrose to the IV fluid when glucose drops below 14 to 17 mmol/L is part of standard DKA management to allow the insulin infusion to continue clearing ketones. However, it is not the immediate response to cerebral oedema, which is the threat to life now. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

Increasing fluids in established DKA-associated cerebral oedema worsens cerebral interstitial fluid accumulation and raises intracranial pressure. The pathway is to reduce fluids and give hyperosmolar therapy. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

CT can be useful but is not the first step; cerebral oedema is a clinical diagnosis in this context and treatment with hyperosmolar therapy must not wait for imaging. Stopping the insulin infusion is unnecessary and will worsen acidosis. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

Dexamethasone has no role in DKA-associated cerebral oedema, which is a non-vasogenic mechanism. The standard hyperosmolar therapy is 3 percent hypertonic saline or mannitol. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines)

The triad of headache, falling heart rate, and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment is cerebral oedema (Cushing response). Immediate management per ISPAD and BSPED guidance is to reduce IV fluid rate by one-third and give hyperosmolar therapy: 3 percent hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes, or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg. Urgent CT after stabilisation is appropriate but treatment is not delayed for imaging. (Source: ISPAD DKA Guidelines; RCH CPG DKA)

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal sepsis with shock and a spreading purpuric rash mandates immediate antibiotics within the first hour after blood cultures and IV or IO access, plus a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, or progressive purpuric rash. LP is deferred until the child is haemodynamically stable. IM benzylpenicillin is reserved for the field when IV or IO access is not available.
key_points: Antibiotics within the first hour of recognition, after cultures.
LP contraindications: shock, raised ICP, coagulopathy, progressive purpuric rash.
Fluid resuscitation: 20 mL/kg crystalloid, repeat to 60 mL/kg before inotropes.
IM benzylpenicillin only when IV or IO access is not available.
explanation.pearls: Give IV or IO ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg in the first hour of suspected meningococcal sepsis and defer LP until the child is haemodynamically stable; never delay antibiotics for CSF sampling.

options.rationale: Performing LP in shock, raised ICP, coagulopathy, or with a spreading purpuric rash is unsafe. Antibiotics within the first hour are the priority; CSF can still yield useful diagnostic information when sampled later, and PCR retains sensitivity for some time. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

RCH paediatric sepsis pathway places antibiotics within the first hour after blood cultures, regardless of LP status. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy, or progressive purpuric rash. Antibiotics are not delayed pending LP. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis paediatric; RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

IM benzylpenicillin is the field option when IV or IO access cannot be obtained. The team here has IO access available, which permits immediate IV-equivalent administration of broad-spectrum ceftriaxone. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of fluid resuscitation; first-line is volume and antibiotics. Starting a bolus of adrenaline before adequate fluid loading is not in the sepsis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis paediatric)

Dexamethasone is not routinely given for suspected meningococcal sepsis; it has a role in confirmed pneumococcal or Haemophilus meningitis if started with or just before the first dose of antibiotic. Use here delays antibiotic administration. (Source: RCH CPG Meningitis paediatric)

explanation.summary: Any febrile infant under 28 days has a full septic workup (blood culture, urine culture, lumbar puncture) and empirical IV antibiotics covering the neonatal spectrum. AU guidance pairs amoxicillin (for Listeria and group B Streptococcus) with cefotaxime (for Gram-negative cover). Ceftriaxone is avoided in the first 28 days of life because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can cause kernicterus. Antipyretic response is not a reliable rule-out for serious bacterial infection.
key_points: Full septic workup is mandatory for any febrile infant under 28 days.
Empirical antibiotics: IV amoxicillin plus IV cefotaxime.
Ceftriaxone is contraindicated under 28 days (bilirubin displacement, kernicterus risk).
Antipyretic response does not rule out serious bacterial infection.
explanation.pearls: Febrile infant under 28 days gets full septic workup including LP plus empirical IV amoxicillin and cefotaxime; ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of kernicterus risk from bilirubin displacement.

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonatal period (first 28 days) because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can cause kernicterus. Cefotaxime is preferred. Amoxicillin is required to cover Listeria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Any febrile infant under 28 days requires a full septic workup including blood culture, urine culture, and CSF examination, followed by empirical IV antibiotic cover for the neonatal pathogen spectrum. AU guidance pairs amoxicillin (for Listeria and group B Streptococcus) with cefotaxime (Gram-negative cover). Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates due to bilirubin displacement risk. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant; Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Withholding LP and antibiotics in any febrile infant under 28 days is unsafe. The neonatal immune system cannot reliably localise infection, and bacterial meningitis has a high mortality without prompt treatment. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for empirical neonatal sepsis cover and the spectrum of cefalexin does not cover Listeria. CSF must be examined. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)

Antipyretic response is not a reliable rule-out for serious bacterial infection in any age group, and especially not in infants under 28 days. The septic workup proceeds regardless of fever response. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile infant)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends a minimum of 4 hours of observation after the last adrenaline dose for any anaphylaxis, with longer observation when there are risk factors for biphasic reaction. Risk factors include needing two or more adrenaline doses, severe asthma, and severe initial reaction. Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of cases, typically within 6 to 8 hours of the initial reaction. Corticosteroids and antihistamines do not prevent biphasic reactions; observation and a clear action plan with adrenaline autoinjector prescription do.
key_points: Minimum 4 hours observation from the last adrenaline dose.
Risk factors for biphasic reaction: 2 or more adrenaline doses, severe asthma, severe initial reaction.
Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent, typically within 6 to 8 hours.
Steroids and antihistamines do not prevent biphasic anaphylaxis.
explanation.pearls: After paediatric anaphylaxis requiring two adrenaline doses, observe for at least 4 hours from the last dose per ASCIA; biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent and steroids do not prevent them.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Same-day discharge before completing 4 hours of post-adrenaline observation does not allow for detection of a biphasic reaction. The risk is highest in patients who needed more than one dose, which applies here. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: ASCIA recommends a minimum 4 hours of observation after the last adrenaline dose for any anaphylaxis. He received two doses (the second 18 minutes ago), so the clock restarts from the second dose. Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of cases, typically within 6 to 8 hours. Children who received 2 or more adrenaline doses are at higher risk and may warrant longer observation. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Routine 24-hour admission is not required for anaphylaxis. A minimum 4-hour observation after the last adrenaline dose, with longer for high-risk features (two or more doses, severe asthma, severe initial reaction, remote location), is the AU standard. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions and are not recommended as monotherapy for prevention. The mainstay is observation and a clear emergency action plan. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.rationale: Antihistamines treat skin symptoms only and have no role in preventing or treating airway or cardiovascular components of anaphylaxis. Their use as monotherapy for discharge planning understates the risk. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: Differential SpO2 (pre-ductal higher than post-ductal) and a four-limb BP gradient (upper limb higher than lower limb) in a collapsing neonate at 5 to 10 days of life indicate duct-dependent coarctation. PGE1 infusion 5 to 50 ng/kg/min is the immediate intervention to reopen or maintain ductal patency. Antibiotics for possible sepsis can be given in parallel but are not the upstream therapy.
key_points: Pre versus post-ductal SpO2 difference indicates a duct-dependent right-to-left or systemic-supply lesion.
PGE1 dose: 5 ng/kg/min, titrated up to 50 ng/kg/min if no response.
Apnoea is a common side effect; have intubation equipment ready.
20 mL/kg bolus is too much for closing-duct shock; use 10 mL/kg if needed.
explanation.pearls: Collapsing 1-week-old with absent femorals, pre versus post-ductal SpO2 gradient, and four-limb BP gradient = duct-dependent coarctation; commence PGE1 5 ng/kg/min and arrange retrieval to a paediatric cardiac centre.

sources.label: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Diuresis without re-establishing ductal flow worsens the obstructive picture. PGE1 first, then supportive care including selective diuresis once the duct is patent and pulmonary congestion is documented. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: A standard 20 mL/kg fluid bolus in undifferentiated neonatal shock can precipitate decompensation if the underlying lesion is left-sided obstruction with a closing duct. Smaller volumes (10 mL/kg) given cautiously plus immediate PGE1 are the AU paediatric cardiology pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Inotropes without restoring ductal flow do not address the obstruction at the aortic isthmus. PGE1 is the upstream intervention; inotropes are an adjunct after ductal flow is re-established. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: While sepsis is a reasonable differential, the four-limb blood pressure gradient and pre versus post-ductal saturation difference strongly point to a duct-dependent cardiac lesion. Antibiotics are appropriate as adjunct cover after PGE1 is started. Ceftriaxone is also relatively contraindicated under 28 days. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

options.rationale: Pre- versus post-ductal SpO2 differential and the four-limb blood pressure gradient indicate duct-dependent coarctation of the aorta. The patent ductus arteriosus is supplying flow to the lower body; once it closes the infant deteriorates rapidly. PGE1 reopens or maintains ductal patency at 5 to 50 ng/kg/min while retrieval is organised to a paediatric cardiac centre. (Source: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Circumferential full-thickness burns can cause external constriction once oedema accumulates, compromising distal perfusion. Indicators include prolonged capillary refill, Doppler-only pulses, firm compartments, and cool extremity. Bedside escharotomy through the insensate eschar restores perfusion and is urgent.
key_points: Escharotomy is bedside, through full-thickness eschar (insensate), no general anaesthesia required.
Indications: circumferential burn plus distal perfusion compromise.
Fasciotomy is separate, for compartment syndrome after escharotomy fails.
Over-resuscitation worsens outcomes; do not chase pulses with fluid alone.
explanation.pearls: Circumferential full-thickness burn with cool distal limb, Doppler-only pulses, and firm compartments needs bedside escharotomy now per ANZBA; elevation, more fluid, and dressings do not relieve eschar constriction.

sources.label: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.rationale: Escharotomy is performed at the bedside through the eschar, which is insensate; it does not require general anaesthesia. Fasciotomy is a different procedure indicated for true compartment syndrome and is performed after escharotomy fails to restore perfusion. Transfer should not delay escharotomy. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.rationale: Limb elevation does not relieve external constriction from the eschar. Once perfusion is compromised, escharotomy is needed urgently; an additional hour of ischaemia risks permanent injury. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.rationale: Increasing fluids does not address mechanical external constriction by full-thickness eschar; it risks over-resuscitation, which is associated with abdominal compartment syndrome and worsened outcomes in burns. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.rationale: Circumferential full-thickness burn with reduced distal perfusion, prolonged capillary refill, Doppler-only pulses, and firm compartments is an indication for urgent escharotomy. The procedure is performed at the bedside through devitalised eschar to relieve external constriction; it does not require theatre time. Delaying for transfer or further investigation risks limb loss. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

options.rationale: Topical dressings address microbial colonisation, not external mechanical constriction. Delaying intervention for 4 hours in an ischaemic limb risks irreversible injury. (Source: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns)
source_refs: ANZBA Emergency Management of Severe Burns

explanation.summary: A femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant carries a high probability of inflicted injury. The combined workup includes admission for safety, full skeletal survey, retinal examination, neuroimaging if indicated, and coagulation studies, with mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. The hospital child protection team coordinates the multidisciplinary response.
key_points: Femoral fracture in non-mobile infant is a major red flag for inflicted injury.
Standard work-up: skeletal survey, ophthalmology, neuroimaging if indicated, coagulation.
Mandatory notification is a legal obligation in all Australian jurisdictions.
Investigation of organic bone disease runs in parallel with safeguarding, not before it.
explanation.pearls: Spiral femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant triggers skeletal survey within 24 hours, retinal exam, coagulation work-up, and statutory notification per RCH CPG; do not delay protection for organic differential workup.

options.rationale: A femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant has a high specificity for inflicted injury. The work-up includes admission for safety, full skeletal survey within 24 hours, ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhage screening, neuroimaging if indicated by age and clinical features, coagulation studies, and mandatory notification to the statutory child protection authority. The hospital child protection team coordinates this. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical; Australian Mandatory Reporting Frameworks)

Discharging without safeguarding workup or notification ignores a strong red flag (femoral fracture in non-mobile infant). The fracture also alone is not the indication for early discharge; the safety risk is. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

Phaeochromocytoma does not cause fragile bones and is not part of the differential for an isolated femoral spiral fracture. Investigation should be guided by the differential of organic causes of bone fragility, not by unrelated rare diseases. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

Outpatient follow-up does not protect the child or initiate the safeguarding pathway. Suspected non-accidental injury requires inpatient assessment to coordinate skeletal survey and child protection involvement. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

Organic bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta, copper deficiency) is part of the differential and is considered during the workup, but notification of suspected abuse does not wait for these results when the index of suspicion is high. Notification and protection run in parallel with differential investigation. (Source: RCH CPG Child abuse - physical)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is managed against gestational age and post-natal age-specific thresholds for phototherapy and exchange transfusion. Above the phototherapy line, intensive phototherapy is commenced with bilirubin rechecked in 6 hours. Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels near or above the exchange threshold despite phototherapy or encephalopathy. Breastfeeding continues throughout.
key_points: Use gestational age + post-natal age treatment threshold charts (e.g. AAP nomogram or RCH paeds jaundice chart).
Intensive phototherapy is first-line above the phototherapy line.
Exchange transfusion is for bilirubin near or above the exchange line, or for encephalopathy.
Continue breastfeeding; supplement if intake is inadequate.
explanation.pearls: Total bilirubin above the gestational and age-specific phototherapy line with positive DAT-driven haemolysis needs intensive phototherapy and a 6-hour bilirubin recheck per RCH CPG; do not cease breastfeeding.

sources.label: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is no longer recommended for breast milk jaundice. AU and international guidance continues breastfeeding with supplementation if intake is inadequate. Cessation undermines establishment of lactation. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold despite intensive phototherapy, or in the presence of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. The current bilirubin of 340 micromol/L is well below the exchange threshold of 430. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Total serum bilirubin above the gestational and age-specific phototherapy line, with positive DAT indicating haemolysis, is an indication for intensive phototherapy. AU practice continues breastfeeding (with supplementation if intake is inadequate) and rechecks bilirubin within 6 hours to monitor response. Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin near or above the exchange line despite intensive phototherapy or in the presence of encephalopathy. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: Home phototherapy is reserved for selected lower-risk presentations and is not first choice when bilirubin is above the inpatient phototherapy threshold and there is evidence of haemolysis. Inpatient intensive phototherapy with monitoring is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.rationale: The bilirubin is above the phototherapy threshold and there is biochemical haemolysis (positive DAT, reticulocytosis). This is not physiological jaundice and observation alone is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy)
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: Sick day rules in Type 1 diabetes mandate continuation of basal insulin throughout intercurrent illness. Rapid-acting insulin correction doses are added for raised ketones (typically 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose). Meals are substituted with sugar-containing fluids when solid food is not tolerated. Omitting basal insulin is the most common precipitant of DKA in established disease and the most important sick day error to correct in parents.
key_points: Never omit basal insulin during illness.
Correction doses with rapid-acting insulin: 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose when ketones above 1.5 mmol/L.
Substitute meals with sugar-containing fluids if not tolerating solids.
Re-present for vomiting, rising ketones, abdominal pain, or drowsiness.
explanation.pearls: T1DM sick day rules: continue basal insulin, give 10 to 20 percent total daily dose as rapid-acting correction for ketones, substitute carbohydrate-containing fluids for solid meals; omitting basal is the most common DKA precipitant.

options.rationale: Discharge with insulin omission is unsafe. Sick day rules require continuation of basal insulin, with correction doses for raised ketones, and clear advice to re-present if vomiting worsens or ketones rise. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

Omitting basal insulin is the most common precipitant of DKA in established Type 1 diabetes during intercurrent illness. The insulin requirement is often higher, not lower, during illness because of counter-regulatory hormones. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

Reducing basal insulin in the presence of raised ketones and intercurrent illness worsens insulinopenia and risks DKA. The opposite approach (continue basal, add correction doses) is correct. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

IV insulin infusion is reserved for established DKA (pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18). This patient has ketosis without DKA and can be managed with subcutaneous insulin per sick day rules. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

Sick day rules in Type 1 diabetes are explicit: never omit basal insulin even when not eating, give correction doses of rapid-acting insulin (typically 10 to 20 percent of total daily dose) for raised ketones, and substitute meals with sugar-containing fluids if solid food is not tolerated. Omitting basal precipitates DKA. (Source: ISPAD Sick Day Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sudden-onset severe testicular pain with high-riding horizontal lie and absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion. Surgical exploration within 6 hours of symptom onset maximises salvage; imaging or antibiotic trial is not appropriate when the clinical picture is typical. Both testes are fixed at surgery because of the bell-clapper anatomy.
key_points: Classic torsion: sudden pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex.
Salvage window is best within 6 hours of symptom onset.
Doppler ultrasound is reserved for equivocal presentations.
Both testes are fixed at surgery due to bell-clapper anomaly.
explanation.pearls: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis; take to theatre for scrotal exploration and bilateral orchidopexy within 6 hours of symptom onset rather than delaying for Doppler ultrasound.

options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound has good sensitivity but is operator-dependent and false-negative results occur. When the clinical picture is classic for torsion, surgical exploration is not delayed for imaging. Ultrasound is reserved for equivocal cases. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)

Sudden-onset severe testicular pain with high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. Surgical exploration must occur within 6 hours of symptom onset to maximise testicular salvage. Imaging that delays surgery is unsafe; clinical diagnosis triggers theatre directly. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance; RCH CPG Acute scrotum)

Epididymo-orchitis typically has a more gradual onset, urinary symptoms, and a normal cremasteric reflex. Antibiotic trial in a presentation classic for torsion wastes the salvage window. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)

Manual detorsion can be considered when there is a substantial delay before theatre, but it is not a substitute for surgical exploration; success rate is variable and confirmation of resolution still requires operative fixation of both testes within the same admission. (Source: AUA paediatric urology guidance)
Discharge from the emergency department for a high-suspicion torsion presentation is unsafe and leads to testicular loss. (Source: RCH CPG Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Risk stratification after Kawasaki disease turns on the six to eight week echocardiogram. A child whose coronary arteries have never been abnormal and whose inflammatory markers have normalised sits in the lowest risk group: aspirin stops, no activity restriction applies, and no ongoing cardiology follow-up is required beyond routine care. Children with transient dilatation that has resolved are usually imaged once more before discharge, and children with persisting aneurysms move onto lifelong follow-up with antiplatelet therapy, periodic imaging and, for giant aneurysms, anticoagulation and exercise restriction. Counselling about long-term cardiovascular risk factors remains sensible for all of them. In context, Kawasaki disease is an acute self-limiting vasculitis, so most children are genuinely cured, and over-medicalising the low risk group with indefinite aspirin and open-ended surveillance is its own harm.
key_points: Normal coronary arteries at six to eight weeks defines the lowest risk group.
Low risk children stop aspirin with no activity restriction.
Persisting aneurysms mean lifelong antiplatelet therapy and cardiology follow-up.
Exercise restriction and stress testing belong to large and giant aneurysms only.
explanation.pearls: The clearance decision needs both a normal echocardiogram and normalised inflammatory markers; a persistently raised ESR at six weeks should prompt a closer look before aspirin is stopped.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Normal coronary arteries at six to eight weeks with settled inflammatory markers defines the lowest risk group, who stop aspirin and need no cardiology surveillance or activity restriction. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Indefinite antiplatelet therapy with annual review is the plan for a child left with persisting coronary dilatation or aneurysms. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Activity restriction and stress testing apply to children with large or giant aneurysms, in whom myocardial ischaemia is a real risk. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Swapping antiplatelet agents is considered for salicylate intolerance or for dual therapy in moderate aneurysms, not for a child being discharged from surveillance. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: A twelve-month study would be scheduled if the six to eight week imaging had shown dilatation that needed tracking to resolution. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

explanation.summary: Paediatric community-acquired pneumonia is most often pneumococcal in vaccinated under-five Australians. Admission triggers under RCH guidance include SpO2 less than 92 percent, significant respiratory distress, dehydration or inability to feed, and toxic appearance. Inpatient first line therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin, switching to oral amoxicillin once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours. Reserve ceftriaxone for complicated disease or treatment failure.
key_points: Admission criteria: SpO2 < 92 percent, severe distress, dehydration, toxic appearance, age under 3 months, or social concerns
Inpatient first line: IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every six hours
Step down to oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours
Total course 5 to 7 days for uncomplicated lobar pneumonia
Add macrolide if atypical features (school age, dry cough, headache, interstitial pattern)
explanation.pearls: Reduced breath sounds with stony dullness despite IV benzylpenicillin for 48 hours prompts urgent chest ultrasound to detect early parapneumonic effusion before clinical decompensation.

options.rationale: Australian first line inpatient therapy for typical bacterial CAP in a vaccinated child is intravenous benzylpenicillin; switch to oral amoxicillin once afebrile for 24 to 48 hours. The SpO2 of 92 percent with feeding compromise and tachypnoea satisfies admission criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

Hypoxia (SpO2 less than 93 percent), tachypnoea above 50 in this age band, and reduced oral intake mandate inpatient management under RCH criteria. Oral therapy is appropriate only when these admission triggers are absent. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe disease, suspected resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, complications such as empyema, or failure of penicillin therapy. Routine empirical use drives resistance and is not first line in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Mycoplasma is uncommon under five years and lobar consolidation favours typical bacterial pathogens. Macrolide monotherapy misses Streptococcus pneumoniae and is not first line in this age band. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Withholding antibiotics in a hypoxic febrile child with lobar consolidation risks progression and empyema. Viral PCR and procalcitonin are adjuncts and do not justify treatment delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Intussusception is the commonest abdominal emergency between three months and three years. The classic triad of colicky pain, palpable mass, and redcurrant stools occurs in fewer than 20 percent, so a high index of suspicion is needed. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice (target or doughnut sign). Air enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 90 percent of stable children, with surgery reserved for failure, perforation, peritonism, or pathological lead points.
key_points: Peak incidence 3 months to 3 years; ileocolic most common
Ultrasound target sign is the diagnostic test
Air enema first line if stable, no peritonism, no perforation
Nasogastric decompression and 20 mL/kg fluid bolus before reduction
Recurrence after enema reduction is around 10 percent and may need repeat enema or surgery
explanation.pearls: After successful air enema reduction at the RCH, recurrence within 72 hours is around 10 percent, so admit for at least 24 hours of observation rather than same-day discharge.

options.rationale: Abdominal radiography is insensitive for intussusception and discharge is unsafe with the diagnosis already confirmed on ultrasound. Untreated ileocolic intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Primary laparotomy is reserved for peritonism, perforation on imaging, shock that does not respond to resuscitation, or failed radiological reduction. None of these are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Air enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance is the first line treatment for ileocolic intussusception in a haemodynamically stable child without peritonism or perforation. Success rates exceed 80 percent and surgery is reserved for failure or complications. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)
Observation alone allows ongoing bowel ischaemia. Definitive reduction must occur as soon as resuscitation allows. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

Empirical antibiotics and primary laparoscopy bypass radiological reduction which is non-invasive and highly effective. Antibiotics are added only when perforation or established sepsis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Australian doctors are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse under state and territory legislation. Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury and demands a structured non-accidental injury workup: skeletal survey (repeat in two weeks), retinal examination by ophthalmology, head imaging, coagulation screen, and social work involvement. Reasonable suspicion, not proof, is the threshold for notification.
key_points: Pre-mobile infants ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') with bruising warrant a full NAI workup
Notify state child protection on reasonable suspicion - not after exclusion of bleeding diatheses
Skeletal survey is standard; repeat in two weeks improves sensitivity for healing fractures
Document carefully, photograph injuries with consent, escalate to senior paediatrics and social work
Coagulation studies and platelet function tests run in parallel, not before reporting
explanation.pearls: In Australian state law (including Children and Young People Act variants), the threshold for mandatory notification is reasonable suspicion of significant harm - higher than 'possible' but lower than 'probable on the balance of probabilities'.

sources.label: RACGP: Abuse and violence working with our patients in general practice

options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant is a sentinel injury for non-accidental injury and discharge is unsafe. Cumulative risk of further inflicted injury or death within months of a missed sentinel bruise is well described. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Bruising in a non-cruising infant is not normal and iron studies have no diagnostic role. Outpatient deferral allows continued exposure to a potentially unsafe environment. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Coagulation studies are part of the workup but do not delay mandatory reporting. Statutory notification is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not by exclusion of bleeding disorders. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Bruising in a pre-mobile infant ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') mandates reporting to the state child protection service and a complete non-accidental injury workup including skeletal survey, retinal examination, head imaging, and consideration of a coagulation screen. Australian medical practitioners are mandated reporters in every state and territory. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

Statutory notification is mandatory once reasonable suspicion arises and does not require parental admission or denial. Delaying notification undermines the protective intent of the legislation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: The 'critical sample' drawn at the moment of hypoglycaemia is the most informative investigation in a paediatric hypoglycaemia workup because it preserves the metabolic snapshot. Appropriate ketosis with suppressed insulin and intact counter-regulation defines idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia, a diagnosis of exclusion peaking between 18 months and 5 years and self-limiting by school age. The cornerstone of management is avoidance of prolonged fasting and early carbohydrate during intercurrent illness.
key_points: Critical sample: glucose, ketones, free fatty acids, insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, GH, lactate, ammonia, urine organic acids, acylcarnitines
Hyperinsulinism: hypoketotic, hypo-lipolytic, detectable insulin/C-peptide
Fatty acid oxidation defect: hypoketotic with high free fatty acids
GSD1: hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidaemia
Adrenal insufficiency: cortisol < 500 nmol/L at the time of hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia is a diagnosis of exclusion - if hypoglycaemia first occurs after age 5, MCAD or another fatty acid oxidation disorder must be actively excluded by acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids before applying the label.

sources.label: APEG: Paediatric Endocrine Society of Australia (APEG) Hypoglycaemia

options.rationale: MCAD presents with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia because fatty acid oxidation is blocked. The high 3-hydroxybutyrate effectively excludes a fatty acid oxidation defect at presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Hyperinsulinism produces hypoketotic and non-lipolytic hypoglycaemia with detectable insulin and C-peptide at the time of low glucose. The high ketones, free fatty acids, and suppressed insulin here exclude this. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Fasting hypoglycaemia with appropriate ketosis and lipolysis, suppressed insulin and C-peptide, and a robust cortisol and growth hormone response is the textbook profile of idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia, peak age 18 months to 5 years. The provocation (vomiting and reduced overnight intake in a thin toddler) fits. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

GSD1 features hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis with hypoglycaemia, and elevated triglycerides and uric acid. Absent hepatomegaly and a normal lactate at the time of hypoglycaemia argue against this diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

Adrenal insufficiency produces hypoglycaemia with an inappropriately low cortisol (under 500 nmol/L) at the time of the event. The cortisol of 612 nmol/L documents a normal stress response. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA is defined by pH less than 7.3 or bicarbonate less than 15, hyperglycaemia, and ketonaemia. The greatest threat is cerebral oedema, which carries roughly 25 percent mortality and 35 percent neurological morbidity. Modern Australian protocols (APEG, RCH) align with ISPAD: cautious rehydration with one 10 mL/kg saline bolus (only repeat for shock), insulin no earlier than one hour after fluid commencement at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, deficit replacement over 48 hours, hourly neuro observations, and bicarbonate only for arrest or severe hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Diagnose DKA: pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15, glucose > 11, ketones > 3 mmol/L
Single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus for moderate-severe DKA without shock
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour from one hour after fluid started
Replace deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours
Cerebral oedema warning signs: headache, falling Glasgow Coma Score, hypertension, bradycardia - give 2.7 percent saline or mannitol immediately
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA peaks 4 to 12 hours after starting fluids - hourly neurological observations and a low threshold for hypertonic saline 2.7 percent at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg are mandatory.

options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg boluses are reserved for shock; this child has compensated tachycardia and capillary refill three seconds (consistent with around 7 to 10 percent dehydration but not shocked). Bolusing 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes risks cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

The total deficit plus maintenance is replaced evenly over 48 hours in paediatric DKA. Six hour replacement accelerates osmotic shifts and increases the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

Insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation causes a rapid intracellular potassium shift, intravascular volume depletion, and increases cerebral oedema risk. Australian protocols require fluid first and insulin no earlier than one hour after fluid commencement. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or cardiac arrest unresponsive to standard resuscitation. It worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CSF acidosis. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

APEG/ISPAD-aligned RCH protocols give a single 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes for moderate to severe DKA without shock, withhold insulin for the first hour to allow rehydration, then commence insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour. This minimises rapid osmotic shifts and cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Any infant under three months with a documented fever of 38.0 degrees or above requires a full septic workup (full blood count, blood culture, urine culture, lumbar puncture, chest radiograph if respiratory features) and empirical intravenous antibiotics in Australia. The pathogen profile is age dependent: Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria dominate under one month; pneumococcus and meningococcus rise after one month. Cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover) is the empirical regimen for under-four-weeks; cefotaxime alone after that.
key_points: Fever 38.0 or above under three months mandates full septic workup including LP
Under 4 weeks: cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours plus amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin for Listeria
4 weeks to 3 months: cefotaxime alone usually adequate; reassess for Listeria risk
Positive viral PCR does NOT exclude concurrent serious bacterial infection
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid alone is inadequate; cephalosporins do not cover Listeria
