explanation.pearls: Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins - cover Listeria with amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin in any febrile infant under four weeks, even when cefotaxime is already running.

options.rationale: Infants under three months with fever cannot be discharged based on a single short observation. Bacterial meningitis and bacteraemia are missed by relying on clinical appearance alone in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers Group B Streptococcus and Listeria but provides inadequate cover for Gram negative meningitis in a 4-week-old. RCH and Therapeutic Guidelines specify cefotaxime (with amoxicillin/ampicillin for Listeria cover if under one month) as the empirical choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

Deferring lumbar puncture in a febrile infant under three months risks missing meningitis (cell counts and protein normalise within hours of antibiotic exposure). Flucloxacillin/gentamicin misses pneumococcal and listerial cover. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

Infants under four weeks with fever require a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin or benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes (which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins). After 4 weeks, cefotaxime monotherapy is generally adequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

A positive viral PCR does not exclude concurrent serious bacterial infection in this age group; up to 7 percent of febrile infants under three months with a positive viral PCR also have a serious bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant)

explanation.summary: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS, secondary HLH) complicates around 10 percent of systemic JIA. The diagnostic signature is extreme hyperferritinaemia (often greater than 10000 mcg/L), a paradoxical fall in ESR despite high CRP, falling platelets and white cells, rising triglycerides, falling fibrinogen, transaminitis, and hyponatraemia. Untreated mortality approaches 20 percent. First line treatment is pulse methylprednisolone with anakinra (IL-1 blocker) as steroid-sparing; ciclosporin is added for refractory disease. Recognition requires actively considering MAS in any sJIA child with worsening fever, falling counts, or rising ferritin.
key_points: Quotidian (once daily) fever with evanescent salmon rash is sJIA
MAS signature: ferritin > 10000, falling ESR with rising CRP, low fibrinogen, high triglycerides, transaminitis, hyponatraemia
First line MAS: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day pulses with anakinra 2 to 4 mg/kg/day
Differentiated from KD by quotidian fever, evanescent rash, lack of coronary involvement, IVIG resistance
PRINTO 2016 MAS classification criteria operationalise the laboratory pattern
explanation.pearls: Ferritin above 10000 mcg/L in a child with persistent inflammation has a positive likelihood ratio above 50 for MAS - escalate to pulse methylprednisolone and anakinra without waiting for bone marrow haemophagocytosis.

sources.label: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA
RCH CPG: Fever of Unknown Origin

options.rationale: Persistent quotidian fever with evanescent rash and falling ESR despite rising ferritin is not the Kawasaki pattern, and the absence of mucocutaneous features now (with normal coronaries on day 7) argues against KD. IVIG resistance in true KD would still show coronary inflammation or partial mucocutaneous response. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.rationale: Quotidian fever with evanescent salmon rash, hepatosplenomegaly, an inflammatory knee effusion, IVIG resistance, and the laboratory signature of MAS (extreme hyperferritinaemia, falling platelets and ESR, rising triglycerides, falling fibrinogen, transaminitis, hyponatraemia) define sJIA-MAS. The 'paradoxical fall' in ESR with persistently high ferritin is highly suggestive. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.rationale: ALL typically produces pancytopenia with circulating blasts, marrow failure, and bone pain rather than the inflammatory cytokine storm shown here. The neutrophilia of 19.8, very high ferritin, and triglyceride rise fit MAS, not leukaemia. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.rationale: Visceral leishmaniasis is rare in non-endemic Australian children and the absence of travel history makes it improbable. Secondary HLH from infection would still need Leishmania exposure that is not described. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

options.rationale: PFAPA presents with recurrent stereotyped fever episodes (every 3 to 6 weeks lasting 3 to 5 days) with pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers, and adenitis - a fundamentally different temporal pattern with normal laboratories between episodes. (Source: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA)
source_refs: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health: Systemic JIA

explanation.summary: Croup severity in Australian paediatric practice is graded by stridor pattern, work of breathing, and conscious state. Mild and moderate croup get a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. Severe croup gets dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline and intensive monitoring. After nebulised adrenaline, observe for at least three hours to detect rebound stridor before discharge.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose
Severe croup: oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Minimum three hour observation after last nebulised adrenaline
Prednisolone is inferior to dexamethasone (higher relapse)
Drooling or stridor with toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis instead
explanation.pearls: Stridor at rest with mild recession but a smiling drinking child is moderate croup and the correct dexamethasone dose is 0.15 mg/kg, not 0.6 mg/kg.

options.rationale: Stridor at rest with only mild recession in a child who is alert, drinking, and not exhausted classifies as moderate croup, for which RCH recommends a single 0.15 mg/kg dose of oral dexamethasone with observation; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

The 0.6 mg/kg dose and intensive care notification are reserved for severe croup with marked recession, tracheal tug, exhaustion, or cyanosis. This child does not meet those criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup; mild and moderate disease do not require it. RCH specifies a minimum three hour observation period (not four) after the last nebulised adrenaline dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Prednisolone has higher relapse and re-presentation rates than single dose dexamethasone for croup and is not preferred in the RCH protocol. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)
Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure with exhaustion or cyanosis despite nebulised adrenaline. This child is alert, drinking, and saturating well. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Paediatric gastroenteritis rehydration in Australia follows a stepped pathway based on dehydration severity. Mild to moderate dehydration that fails oral rehydration solution at home is treated in hospital with nasogastric rehydration as first line. A single dose of ondansetron facilitates oral or nasogastric tolerance. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure.
key_points: Mild-moderate dehydration that fails oral: nasogastric rehydration is first line
Single dose oral ondansetron: 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg
Intravenous fluids only for severe dehydration, shock, or nasogastric failure
Anti-motility agents (loperamide) are contraindicated
Empirical antibiotics not indicated for routine viral gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: Failed home oral rehydration solution plus moderate dehydration is the textbook indication for a single 2 mg ondansetron wafer plus nasogastric rehydration over four hours, not intravenous cannulation.

options.rationale: Rapid intravenous bolus rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration with shock features (prolonged capillary return greater than three seconds, hypotension, depressed conscious state). This child has mild to moderate dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Home oral rehydration has already failed because of vomiting and refusal. Discharging without an in-department intervention risks ongoing decline and a repeat presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Single dose ondansetron (2 mg for 8 to 15 kg per RCH) reduces vomiting and admission rates. Nasogastric rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration with failed oral therapy and is non-inferior to intravenous fluids while avoiding cannulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Anti-motility agents are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis because of the risk of toxic megacolon and masking of bacterial colitis. They have no role in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

Empirical antibiotics are not indicated in suspected viral gastroenteritis without bloody stool, sepsis, or specific risk factors. Stool PCR does not change immediate rehydration management. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric anaphylaxis adrenaline dosing follows the ASCIA banded table by weight rather than per-kilogram arithmetic, which reduces calculation errors during resuscitation. The 7.5 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms of 1:1000 solution intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh, repeatable every five minutes. EpiPen Junior delivers this dose; EpiPen delivers 300 micrograms for 20 kg and above.
key_points: Use ASCIA banded adrenaline table, not mg/kg arithmetic
7.5-20 kg: 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr); 20+ kg: 300 micrograms (EpiPen)
Adrenaline 1:1000, intramuscular, anterolateral thigh
Repeat every five minutes for ongoing reaction
Intravenous adrenaline reserved for arrest or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: For a 16 kg child in anaphylaxis the ASCIA banded dose is 150 micrograms of 1:1000 intramuscular, equivalent to an EpiPen Junior, not 0.16 mL of 1:1000 calculated by 10 micrograms per kg.

options.rationale: Anaphylaxis adrenaline is 1:1000, not 1:10000, and the ASCIA banded dosing table is preferred over per-kilogram arithmetic to reduce dosing error in the resuscitation environment. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) is the adult and over 50 kg dose. A 16 kg child receives 150 micrograms by the ASCIA banded table. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory anaphylaxis on a senior clinician decision. Intramuscular adrenaline is first line and faster to deliver. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

Subcutaneous adrenaline absorption is unreliable in anaphylaxis with peripheral shutdown; intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh is the recommended route. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

The ASCIA banded paediatric dose for 7.5 to 20 kg is 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1:1000) intramuscular into the anterolateral thigh, repeatable every five minutes for ongoing reaction. (Source: ASCIA Acute Anaphylaxis Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Measles and Kawasaki disease overlap on fever of four or more days, non-purulent conjunctivitis and a widespread rash, and both occur in the preschool years. The prodrome and the blood count separate them: measles brings cough and coryza, a buccal enanthem, a rash that starts on the face and spreads downwards, and leucopenia, while Kawasaki disease brings mucosal and peripheral changes, marked neutrophilia and rising platelets. Travel to a country with ongoing transmission and the absence of immunisation shift the odds further. Management is therefore public health rather than pharmacological: airborne isolation on arrival, nasopharyngeal swab and urine for PCR with paired serology, immediate telephone notification to the local public health unit, and vitamin A for the child. In context, measles remains eliminated in Australia only through imported case containment, so recognising it in the department and isolating before the diagnosis is confirmed is the decision that prevents an outbreak.
key_points: Cough, coryza and an enanthem separate measles from Kawasaki disease.
Leucopenia points to measles; neutrophilia and thrombocytosis to Kawasaki disease.
Measles is urgently notifiable by telephone in New South Wales.
Airborne isolation starts on clinical suspicion, not on the PCR result.
explanation.pearls: Ask about the rash sequence: a rash that began on the face behind the ears and moved down the trunk is measles until proven otherwise, and the child has already been infectious for four days.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, buccal enanthem and a descending rash in an unimmunised returned traveller is measles, an urgently notifiable disease in New South Wales requiring airborne isolation, PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab and immediate telephone notification so contacts can be traced. (Source: NSW Health Measles Control Guideline)

Immunoglobulin and aspirin would be right for Kawasaki disease, which shares the fever, conjunctivitis and rash but has no cough or coryza, no enanthem of this kind and a raised rather than low white cell count. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Urgent coronary imaging belongs to suspected complete or incomplete Kawasaki disease after five days of otherwise unexplained fever. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Kawasaki disease

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics and cerebrospinal fluid sampling are indicated for suspected invasive bacterial infection, suggested by toxicity, a non-blanching rash or altered conscious state. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.rationale: Community review without isolation would be appropriate for an ordinary self-limiting viral exanthem in an immunised child with no travel history. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Any unwell febrile infant under 28 days receives a full septic workup (blood culture, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid for bacterial and herpes simplex virus studies) and immediate empirical broad spectrum antimicrobials. From 7 to 28 days the Australian regimen is intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover gram negatives, Listeria, and late onset group B streptococcus, plus aciclovir if there is any suggestion of meningitis or encephalitis.
key_points: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture in any unwell infant under 28 days
First week of life: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin empirically
7 to 28 days: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin empirically
Add aciclovir if seizures, encephalopathy, or HSV exposure risk
Ceftriaxone avoided in the first month (bilirubin displacement risk)
explanation.pearls: Substitute cefotaxime for ceftriaxone in the first month of life because ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and precipitates kernicterus in the neonate.

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the antimicrobial pair used during the first week of life. Beyond 7 to 28 days the empirical Australian regimen typically substitutes a third generation cephalosporin to cover community pathogens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Any unwell infant under 28 days requires full septic workup including lumbar puncture and parenteral empirical therapy. Oral amoxicillin is inadequate cover and deferring lumbar puncture is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Watchful waiting in a febrile, poorly perfused 21-day-old with elevated lactate is unsafe. Bacterial sepsis and herpes simplex virus encephalitis can both progress rapidly without antimicrobials. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

An unwell febrile infant aged 7 to 28 days needs a full septic workup including lumbar puncture and immediate empirical cover for late onset group B streptococcal disease (benzylpenicillin), gram negative organisms and Listeria (cefotaxime), and herpes simplex encephalitis (aciclovir). Fluid resuscitation precedes inotropes. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

Ceftriaxone is avoided in the first month because it displaces bilirubin and can precipitate kernicterus. Cefotaxime is preferred. Monotherapy misses Listeria and herpes simplex virus, and dextrose alone does not address shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis is the most common surgical cause of vomiting in the first two months of life and classically presents in a first-born male with non-bilious projectile vomiting, weight loss, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound (pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more). Pyloromyotomy is delayed until biochemistry is corrected to avoid post-operative apnoea from a respiratory compensation for ongoing alkalosis.
key_points: Classical presentation: first-born male, 3-8 weeks, non-bilious projectile vomiting
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Ultrasound: pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more
Correct electrolytes BEFORE pyloromyotomy
Bilious vomiting at any age is malrotation until proven otherwise
explanation.pearls: Pyloromyotomy is deferred until bicarbonate is below 30 mmol/L and chloride is above 100 mmol/L because residual alkalosis drives post-operative apnoea through compensatory hypoventilation.

options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis in a first-born male with projectile non-bilious vomiting at the typical age is classical for pyloric stenosis. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test (pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more). The mass is often not palpable. Surgery only follows full correction of electrolytes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Hypochloraemic alkalosis with weight loss is not consistent with simple gastro-oesophageal reflux. Delay risks worsening dehydration and electrolyte derangement before urgent surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Malrotation with volvulus typically presents with bilious vomiting and is a surgical emergency with an upper gastrointestinal contrast study. This infant has non-bilious projectile vomiting and a metabolic picture pointing to pyloric stenosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting)

Proton pump inhibitor treatment does not address mechanical gastric outlet obstruction and would delay diagnosis. Acid suppression is not the answer to projectile vomiting with weight loss. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

Ultrasound confirmation of pyloric stenosis is required before surgery, and pyloromyotomy is contraindicated until the metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia are corrected to avoid post-operative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric DKA (pH < 7.1, depressed conscious state) carries the highest cerebral oedema risk. APEG and ISPAD recommend a cautious initial 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes and deliberate insulin delay (start at 1 to 2 hours after fluids commence) at 0.05 units/kg/hour, with paediatric retrieval and tertiary transfer. Faster fluid resuscitation and earlier insulin are associated with worse neurological outcomes.
key_points: Severe DKA in children: cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 30-60 min
Delay insulin start by 1-2 hours after fluid commences
Insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour, not 0.1 units/kg/hour
Avoid sodium bicarbonate (worsens cerebral oedema outcomes)
Cerebral oedema warning signs: headache, bradycardia with hypertension, falling GCS
explanation.pearls: In a child with DKA and pH below 7.1 the insulin infusion runs at 0.05 units/kg/hour and only starts 1 to 2 hours after the cautious 10 mL/kg fluid bolus has commenced to minimise osmotic shifts that precede cerebral oedema.

options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg bolus plus immediate insulin in severe paediatric DKA increases cerebral oedema risk through abrupt osmotic shift; the Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group and ISPAD recommend slower initial fluid replacement and delayed insulin in severe DKA. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Severe DKA (pH less than 7.1, GCS depressed) in a child carries the highest cerebral oedema risk. APEG and ISPAD recommend cautious 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 to 60 minutes plus delayed insulin (start at 1 to 2 hours after fluids) at 0.05 units/kg/hour to reduce osmotic shift, and urgent paediatric retrieval. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Sodium bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with worse outcomes including a higher rate of cerebral oedema and is not recommended outside refractory acidosis with cardiovascular compromise unresponsive to fluids. Maintenance-only fluids are inadequate. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Hartmann's and rapid 20 mL/kg are not the recommended initial replacement in severe paediatric DKA; 0.9 percent saline at a slower rate is standard. Insulin commenced concurrently with bolus carries cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

Subcutaneous insulin is unreliable in shock states and oral rehydration is inappropriate in a vomiting child with reduced GCS at risk of aspiration. Intravenous insulin is mandatory once fluids are running. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: This is severe acute asthma with imminent respiratory failure (silent chest, hypercapnia, lactic acidosis) refractory to first-line nebulised bronchodilators plus systemic steroid plus a single dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate. The AU pathway escalates to intravenous bronchodilator therapy next: IV salbutamol is preferred where available, with aminophylline as the AU-listed alternative when salbutamol is unavailable. The regional context decides it: IV salbutamol is not stocked and the retrieval window is 75 minutes, so aminophylline is the right choice despite being second-line at a tertiary centre. The textbook hierarchy (IV salbutamol first) gives way to the practical constraints of stock and retrieval timing, and the available agent is used. In context, escalation pathways must always account for setting and stock; the AU guidelines explicitly preserve aminophylline for this reason.
key_points: AU severe asthma escalation order (RCH Melbourne CPG): nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, systemic steroid, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg, then IV salbutamol OR aminophylline.
IV salbutamol is the AU preferred IV second-line; aminophylline is the AU-listed alternative when IV salbutamol is unavailable.
Aminophylline loading 10 mg/kg over 60 minutes (max 500 mg), maintenance 1 mg/kg/hour, serum theophylline at 2 hours per AMH.
Intubation in paediatric severe asthma is high-risk and is reserved for true cardiorespiratory failure, not as a substitute for IV bronchodilator escalation.
explanation.pearls: Regional ED with retrieval pending often forces aminophylline over IV salbutamol despite the textbook hierarchy; cite the stock + retrieval window explicitly in the team handover.

options.rationale: This child meets imminent respiratory failure criteria (silent chest, rising pCO2, lactic acidosis, exhaustion). IV salbutamol is the preferred AU second-line intravenous agent per the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG and Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory, but the regional pharmacy does not stock it and the retrieval window is 75 minutes. Aminophylline is a valid AU-listed alternative when IV salbutamol is unavailable; both guidelines retain it for this scenario. Loading at 10 mg/kg (280 mg here) over 60 minutes, capped at 500 mg, with continuous cardiac monitoring is the AMH dose and route. Serum theophylline at 2 hours guides the maintenance infusion. (Sources: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; Australian Medicines Handbook)

Intravenous salbutamol is the AU preferred second-line agent when stocked and is generally first-line over aminophylline. However the regional pharmacy does not stock IV salbutamol and the retrieval window is 75 minutes; aminophylline is the appropriate available alternative. Would be the correct first choice in a tertiary centre with IV salbutamol immediately available. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)

A single 50 mg/kg dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate is given and not routinely repeated; further magnesium does not address the persisting bronchospasm and risks hypotension. The next step is a second-line bronchodilator (IV salbutamol or aminophylline). Would be correct only if the patient improved on the first dose and the team wished to bridge a short delay; the AU guidelines do not endorse a routine repeat. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)

Intubation in paediatric severe asthma is high-risk (worsened air-trapping, peri-intubation arrest) and is reserved for true respiratory or cardiorespiratory failure after exhausting non-invasive escalations. The child is still alert and is a candidate for further pharmacological escalation; aminophylline before intubation is the AU pathway. Would be correct only with imminent or actual cardiorespiratory arrest. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute; ANZCOR Paediatric guidelines)

Non-invasive ventilation has a limited and contested role in paediatric acute severe asthma; it does not address the underlying bronchospasm and may delay definitive bronchodilator escalation. Pharmacological escalation (IV aminophylline here) is the AU next step. Would be considered only at a tertiary centre with respiratory team involvement after IV bronchodilator escalation has been exhausted. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Asthma acute)
